items.title: beenuar/AiSOC
items.content:
Open-source AI Security Operations Center: alert fusion, LLM-agent triage, MITRE ATT&CK investigation, and a replayable decision ledger for every agent step. Self-hostable, runs with no API keys, MIT licensed. Ships an MCP server for Claude, Cursor and Continue.

Telemetry arrives from your security tools. AiSOC normalizes it, runs the 2538 executable rules of its 7023-rule library, groups what fires into incidents, investigates each one with an AI agent whose every prompt and tool call is recorded, and proposes an action. New threat intelligence re-sweeps the history you already collected, and a human approves before anything reaches a vendor.

What it looks like running

— install to AI verdict on one server against the published images, terminal waits shortened and the recording saying so on screen. The stills below are from a v20.1.0 run under the same rules — the recording is older than they are. (step by step · what is real)

git clone https://github.com/beenuar/AiSOC && cd AiSOC
make up

, or on a machine with nothing installed yet, one line does the prerequisites too: iwr -useb https://raw.githubusercontent.com/beenuar/AiSOC/main/install.ps1 | iex (curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/beenuar/AiSOC/main/install.sh | bash on Linux and macOS). , pip install aisoc-sandbox && aisoc-sandbox demo walks one alert through the agent funnel offline in under 30 seconds. , open the repo in GitHub Codespaces and run in its terminal. All four end at the same console; only the first three install anything.

The Technical Guide covers this in depth: server sizing, where the model runs, every failure mode with its cause and fix, the REST API, MCP, and every console surface.

Needs Docker Compose v2 with 8 GB memory and 20 GB free disk in the Docker VM, plus (3.9+) and ; checks all of it and Installation says what each number was measured against. The first run downloads a ~2 GB model into a volume only clears.

also creates and generates the secrets in it — the credential vault, the session signing key, five service-to-service credentials and four datastore passwords — then creates an administrator and prints its password, generated on your machine, shown once and stored nowhere. Lost it? make bootstrap ARGS=--reset-password mints another.

A port already in use does not stop the install. AiSOC publishes on a free one, names what held the old one, and moves the console address with it: 64 seconds to a signed-in console on a bare clone with 5432 and 11434 both taken.

Then . posts one real event to the ingest API and follows it through Kafka, detection, correlation and Postgres, then reads the alert back out of the public API. Every stage reports PASS or FAIL:

$ make smoke
[PASS] raw telemetry accepted by ingest
[PASS] event traversed the spine and became an alert
PASS: 10/10 stages

Sign in at the address printed. A tenant with nothing connected lands on a rather than an all-zero dashboard, and its state is read from your own data so it stays right if you connect a source through the API. The spec is — interactive docs are off in this production-class stack. Stuck? , which on a host where you have not run yet says exactly that.

Press in the wizard. Five scenarios take the same ingest path a real connector uses — not inserted rows — so watching them become alerts means watching the pipeline work. They span low to critical on purpose, because a first run where everything is a crisis teaches you nothing about how triage separates signal from routine. They are attributed to in the source column, refuse to load into a tenant that already has real alerts, and do mark setup complete. (what each step proves) For the larger fixed corpus used by demos and evals, loads a dataset — the pipeline shape, never a benchmark, a customer or an incident. Every row is and labelled in the console.

Push, with a credential from (the tenant comes from it, not a header):

curl -X POST http://localhost:8081/v1/ingest/batch \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -H "Authorization: Bearer $AISOC_INGEST_TOKEN" \
  -d '{"connector_id":"edr-1","connector_type":"crowdstrike","events":[{"severity":"high",
       "title":"Encoded PowerShell from Office","host":"WIN-FIN-01"}]}'

Or pull, by configuring one of 90 click-and-connect data connectors in — Splunk, Sentinel, Elastic, CrowdStrike, Okta, AWS and Kubernetes audit among those with vendor-specific normalization and setup docs (coverage). Without a vendor profile a connector still ingests through a generic mapping that resolves host, user and source IP.

A real cloud estate does not hand you its logs over a REST call. Four collectors read the surfaces one actually emits to: a CloudTrail organisation trail on (management events, data events and VPC flow logs), a subscription on a Cloud Logging sink, an capture, and a listener. Each keeps a resumable cursor and a bounded per-poll budget, so a backlog applies backpressure instead of flooding ingest.

Bringing existing detections? translates Splunk SPL, Sentinel KQL and Elastic EQL and refuses rather than approximating what it cannot carry, because an almost-right rule is harder to find than a missing one: of the 2,005 Splunk rules bundled here 1,734 translate and 1,711 of those are partial (what that means).

Ingest normalizes to a common shape and stamps an on every event — actor, action, resource, location, outcome, with read from each vendor's own documented field rather than inferred — then Kafka carries it. Then fusion runs 2538 executable detection rules, of 7023 on disk, plus 76 sliding-window rules (73 count across events; 3 match an ordered sequence), applies on top — the disables, floors and suppressions the console writes, so a rule you turned off actually stops firing — and decides what becomes an alert. Correlation groups related alerts, an agent investigates and writes its reasoning to the Investigation Ledger, and a playbook may start from the result. Separately, new threat intelligence sweeps the lake for sightings you already collected, and a hypothesis becomes a hunt without anyone writing a query — the model fills a closed schema and every value is bound as a parameter, so it cannot express a query at all.

A playbook triggered by an alert previews before it acts. Three switches must agree — the deployment, the tenant, the playbook — and every default is off; anything less runs in preview with its plan attached to the alert. An approval step is a durable pause: the run suspends to Postgres, survives a restart, resumes after the approval, and expires with a recorded outcome rather than hanging.

Executable is earned, not declared. A rule joins the compiled ruleset only after a vendor-shaped event is replayed through the real connector and engine and that rule is — never inferred from a directory or an flag. The proof can fail: reverts the Windows connector and requires all 1,687 Windows rules to go silent. It means reachable, not that it detects an attack. rules still cannot fire — down from 119, because a rule that could not fire stopped being counted as executable — and both are waiting on a behavioural baseline. The ratchet only moves down. (why 1,362 were refused)

Every answer carries its receipts. The copilot cites each checkable claim to the ledger entry behind it and labels the rest rather than dropping them, and any investigation exports as a — byte-identical, prompts as digests, OCSF 1.9.0. (how)

The full alerting pipeline: ingest → detect → correlate → alert → triage → console, plus the LLM gateway, a local model, the CISA KEV threat feed, and the connector and response services the agent's vendor tools reach
Core plus event lake, entity graph, full-text search, enrichment
Core plus labelled synthetic data

CORE is the smallest deployment that takes a real event and produces a real alert, and it needs no credentials to do either.

The model ships with the gateway. Ollama runs a pinned ~2 GB llama3.2:3b-instruct-q4_K_M sized for CPU-only inference, so produces real triage verdicts with real token counts in the Investigation Ledger — not a stub. It is not a frontier model: over 50 alerts it gave triage usable output 44 times before the reply was constrained to JSON and 50 after (method), and the rail labels which path answered. Run it faster with , , or your own provider from the console (all four). No hosted provider has ever been exercised here — there is no funded key, so per-model rows read rather than zero. (ADR-0006)

One real external feed ships too. polls the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog — public, no API key — into the console's Threat Intelligence page: the one thing in a fresh install that is neither synthetic nor yours.

Evaluation, reflex and replay

  • Every verdict scorecard names the model that actually served it — gateway-attested or self-reported, with an explicit provenance status. A run with missing attribution, zero real calls or a deterministic fallback cannot be advertised as a named model's performance, and a measurement that cannot be bound to an attributed call cannot authorize closures.
  • Denominators are published, and the uncomfortable direction wins. Full-cohort recall keeps abstentions and failures in the malicious denominator; closure claims ship with their contamination rate; alert reduction has three labelled figures (75.3% legacy grouping, 33.3% production key, 24.5% on a detection-shaped cohort after a missing identifier was fixed to the group instead of widening it). Unmeasured reads , never .
  • The reflex path is observable — nine named stages from queue delay to verification, and a decision contract carrying supporting evidence, contradictory evidence, missing prerequisites and the escalation reason.
  • Replay is time-frozen; re-hunting is labelled. Historical replay enforces evidence cutoffs in the retrieval queries (never by prompt), discloses the model-knowledge limit, and cannot execute real actions — the mutation boundary is the write adapter. Applying new intelligence to old telemetry is a distinct, rehearsable mode, and its discoveries are never counted as predictions at the original event time.
  • Model suitability is per task. The matrix grades each configured model on the same locked evidence against a deterministic baseline floor (balanced accuracy exactly 0.250); unfunded rows read , with one-command reproduction against any local OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

Agents triage alerts and investigate incidents. What they can and cannot do:

  • the alert, its correlated siblings, entity context, and prior verdicts for the same signature.
  • — lake queries, graph traversals, enrichment lookups. The model picks the tool and passes arguments; it never writes SQL.
  • to the Investigation Ledger — prompts, tool calls, citations, verdict, token cost — and exports as a signed bundle.
  • A verdict citing an indicator the evidence never contained is demoted to human review rather than auto-closed.
  • A prompt is validated before it is sent. Raw logs, OCSF payloads and secret-shaped values are refused, not redacted after the fact.
  • No vendor is touched without a human, unless a tenant has explicitly granted autonomy for that verb. Every response step is graded against its own capability contract at dispatch, so approving a playbook never authorises whatever its steps happen to contain, and an approver must hold the required permission tier and must not be the person who requested the action.

Stable is defined, and a gate enforces it. It was ungated prose until three rows were found describing coverage that did not exist. A row is Stable only with a check that runs on every pull request with no path filter, drives the real production path against real infrastructure, and has a negative control proven by breaking the thing and watching it go red. (the bar)

Ingest → detect → correlate → alert
Detection engine (2538 executable rules) of 7023
Alert correlation into incidents
AI triage + Investigation LedgerLive Postgres ledger + a PR-gated local-model agent run. No hosted provider has been exercised
Event lake + hunting (ClickHouse)Live ClickHouse on the shipped DDL, with a negative control
Retro-hunts when new intel arrivesLive ClickHouse + Kafka with the flag on, with a negative control
68-hunt YAML library, compiled against tenant events in the lakeLive ClickHouse: scheduled hunts read tenant data and refuse to fall back to the fixture; all 114 field names the corpus filters on compile, via a lake column or the stored payload
Live Postgres through the real app: PATCH in both providers' dialects, group membership, deprovisioning proved by its consequences, with a negative control
Live Postgres: the scheduled report and its covering email carry the organisation's brand, with two negative controls
Live ClickHouse on the shipped DDL, with a negative control that makes an unscoped meter fail
Live Neo4j against the production reader, with a negative control
Governed response actionsLive socket: permits, refuses, never leaks a refusal, with a negative control
Alert-triggered playbooks, with a durable approval pauseLive Postgres: suspend, restart, resume, expiry, with a negative controlYes — three opt-ins deep, preview by default
Per-tenant detection tuning in the live engineLive Postgres: tuning written changes what the engine fires, with a negative control
Live scheduler polls a stub vendor into ingest, with a negative control
Live Postgres: migrations, scoring, persistence, isolation, with a negative control
Package distribution (npm/PyPI)The five PyPI packages resolve at the tree's versions, checked against the live registries in both directions with a self-test; the npm half has no registry state to verifypip install aisoc-sandbox (and the other four) works today; the three npm packages still need the first-upload , an account action
  • Not a drop-in SIEM replacement. It correlates and investigates; it does not replace long-term log retention and compliance search.
  • Not able to see telemetry you have not connected. There is no discovery.
  • Not autonomous by default. Response requires explicit policy authorization and a human approver.
  • Demo and sample incidents are not real incidents, and benchmark numbers are substrate self-consistency measures, not live agent accuracy — labelled as such wherever published.

checks host tools, memory, disk, every port and each datastore by it rather than asking whether its container is up, then prints the command to run next. A container killed by a full Docker VM is named as that, not as the service that happened to die. (the six most common failures)

Secrets are generated per deployment and never committed; connector credentials are encrypted at rest. Services connect to Postgres as a DML-only role, so row-level security actually applies, and tenant isolation is enforced at the query layer in every store. RBAC gates every mutating route, ingest is authenticated, and the default install sends no prompt anywhere — the model runs beside it.

SAML and OIDC sign-in with per-connection tenant and group mapping, SCIM provisioning, and console — TOTP with recovery codes, enforceable per tenant. Attribute conditions, time-boxed elevation and workload identities run inside the one permission path, where a condition can only narrow a permission and never grant one. (SSO · access governance)

A service with no credential refuses to serve rather than serving unauthenticated. The changelog records each fix; report via SECURITY.md.

make test        # unit tests for every service
make smoke       # the golden pipeline, against a running stack
make stats       # recount every figure this README publishes

Funding · Roadmap · Contributing · License

Development is funded and supported by , who pay for the engineering time behind AiSOC and release it under the MIT licence rather than keeping it. That buys no special treatment here — no Cyble-only features, no gated modules, no telemetry. (full credits)

items.title: kornia/kornia
items.content:
🐍 Geometric Computer Vision Library for Spatial AI

is a differentiable computer vision library that provides a rich set of differentiable image processing and geometric vision algorithms. Built on top of PyTorch, Kornia integrates seamlessly into existing AI workflows, allowing you to leverage powerful batch transformations, auto-differentiation and GPU acceleration. Whether you're working on image transformations, augmentations, or AI-driven image processing, Kornia equips you with the tools you need to bring your ideas to life.

: Kornia is becoming the reference implementation and executable specification for differentiable computer vision and geometry in the PyTorch ecosystem — explicit conventions, conformance tests, and honest benchmarks over API growth. Read the Roadmap.

Kornia pays off where a hand-written version gets long or fragile, or where the alternatives leave the GPU:

  • 1,200+ public operators, most with no torchvision equivalent: camera models and epipolar geometry, minimal solvers and RANSAC, feature detection, description and matching, edge detection, morphology, Lab and Bayer color, image losses and metrics. torchvision overlaps mainly on resizing, cropping, flipping, color jitter and blur.
  • Per-sample parameters in one batched call.gaussian_blur2d(x, (9, 9), sigma) takes a ; takes a angle, / take / matrices and a factor. torchvision's functional ops apply one parameter per call. From Kornia 0.9.1, a tensor and the enhancement value checks (gamma, contrast, solarize) are validated on the device, so a CUDA call, or an MPS call on PyTorch ≥ 2.13, needs no host synchronization for them.
  • Batched minimal solvers and robust estimation.find_fundamental(x1, x2, method="7POINT") solves samples and returns all real solutions in , with zero matrices in the unused slots; the 8-point, 5-point essential (), DLT homography and PnP () solvers are there too. (homography, fundamental and essential models) samples and scores hypotheses on the device; by default its refinement and final selection run on the host in float64, and (PyTorch ≥ 2.14, CPU and CUDA) runs the whole estimation as one compiled graph on the device.
  • Depth to 3D and back (, , ), , , camera models with Brown–Conrady and Kannala–Brandt distortion, and Lie groups (, ) keep gradients with respect to depth, pose and camera parameters.
  • applies one sampled transform to images, masks, boxes and keypoints together and can invert it, in 2D; the 3D augmentations transform volumes, without annotations or an inverse. On CUDA, augmentations move their sampled parameters to the GPU without blocking it, and a sync-guard test keeps every public augmentation free of avoidable host synchronizations.
  • Local features on the GPU. SIFT and HardNet, DISK, ALIKED, XFeat, DeDoDe, LoFTR and LightGlue, with mutual-nearest-neighbour and ratio-test matchers.
  • with arbitrary structuring elements on batched tensors.
  • Nearly all probed operator configurations run under and match eager, and over 1,000 export to ONNX; the result for every operator is on the export support page.
  • Fast where it is designed to be: batched tensors on a GPU. In the published 0.9.0 flagship benchmarks (RTX 4090, batch 32), many filters, warps, feature-matching steps and image metrics run about 10× to 70× faster in eager mode than per-image OpenCV or scikit-image on the CPU, and takes several of them past 100×. On the small overlap with torchvision on the same GPU, eager Kornia is slower; compiled Kornia is faster for hue, color jitter and Gaussian blur and still slower for flips, crops and brightness. OpenCV wins single-image CPU work. Results vary with hardware and workload; every number, win and loss is published on the performance page.

These operators run on the input's device with no NumPy round trip, and most are differentiable; robust estimation () and the extraction methods of learned features such as DeDoDe and XFeat run without gradients. For a single fixed-parameter operation, such as one blur or one resize, a few lines of PyTorch or torchvision are just as good.

  1. Differentiable Image Processing Kornia provides a comprehensive suite of image processing operators, all differentiable and ready to integrate into deep learning pipelines.
    • : Gaussian, Sobel, Median, Box Blur, etc.
    • : Affine, Homography, Perspective, etc.
    • : Histogram Equalization, CLAHE, Gamma Correction, etc.
    • : Canny, Laplacian, Sobel, etc.
    • ... check our docs for more.
  2. Perform powerful data augmentation with Kornia’s built-in functions, ideal for training AI models with complex augmentation pipelines.
    • : AugmentationSequential, PatchSequential, VideoSequential, etc.
    • : AutoAugment, RandAugment, TrivialAugment.
  3. Leverage pre-trained AI models optimized for a variety of vision tasks, all within the Kornia ecosystem.
    • : LoFTR, LightGlue
    • : DISK, DeDoDe, SOLD2
    • : MobileViT, VisionTransformer.

CUDA and Half-Precision Support

The module table below counts entries in the Linux CPU known-failure manifests (, ), pinned to Python 3.11 and PyTorch 2.15.0. There are 243 float16 and 256 bfloat16 recorded failures. These are parametrized test cases, not counts of unsupported functions. The remaining work is tracked in #4153. No CI job covers CUDA or MPS half precision; CPU results do not establish support on those backends.

Known failures (fp16 / bf16)
Lab/Luv conversions and compute half inputs in float32 and return the input dtype
Canny, Gaussian kernels/blur and CPU FFT convolution compute half inputs in float32 and return the input dtype
ZCA keeps half-input fitted state in float32; whitening and JPEG return the input dtype after float32 computation
float16: container autocast/runtime errors and accuracy; both dtypes: 3D backward and random-generator accuracy
kornia.geometry.transformRotation matrices, affine/perspective warps and homography-warper accuracy
Projection, distortion round trips and stereo reprojection; includes test-side dtype assertions
kornia.geometry.calibrationsolve_pnp_dlt rejects half inputs; undistort_points accuracy
Essential-matrix decomposition/motion and KRt_from_projection lack CPU half kernels; fundamental-matrix accuracy
kornia.geometry.homographyDLT solver accuracy, including iterated and line-based variants
So2/Se2 reject bfloat16 rotation construction: PyTorch has no complex bfloat16 dtype; these expected errors/skips are outside the manifests
SpatialSoftArgmax2d and ConvQuadInterp3d accuracy; bfloat16: render_gaussian2d accuracy
kornia.geometry.conversionsAngle-axis, quaternion and rotation-matrix accuracy; includes tests/integration/test_conversions.py
Essential-model fitting raises in epipolar solvers
Box-transform and depth accuracy
Circle/ellipse polygon-fill comparisons use vertices and reference masks computed in half precision
bfloat16: total-variation accuracy
Matching uses a manual cdist fallback for half dtypes; LightGlue's float16 tests are skipped
bfloat16: RT-DETR RepVGG fusion accuracy
contrib, core, io, onnx, sensors, tracking, utilsbfloat16: histogram matching and _torch_svd_cast accuracy

✅ No entries in the CPU known-failure manifest   ⚠️ Has recorded CPU failures. Neither symbol promises complete dtype support: skips, expected exceptions and source-level xfails are outside these counts. Some operators compute internally in float32 or float64 and return the input dtype.

Observed CPU CI outcomes:

Each job also deselected 3 ONNX conformance tests. XFAIL totals include both the strict manifest entries and source-level expected failures. The 4 XPASSes in each successful job are non-strict expected failures that passed; a passing entry makes verification fail, as do a changed exception, a skipped entry or a stale node ID. A green job therefore means the recorded baseline reproduced, even though known failures and skips remain. These totals describe the linked revision; the module table describes the checked-in manifests.

Verify the complete CPU profiles in the pinned environment with:

KORNIA_TEST_OPTIMIZER= pixi run test-module tests/ --verify-known-failures --known-failure-profile=cpu-float16
KORNIA_TEST_OPTIMIZER= pixi run test-module tests/ --verify-known-failures --known-failure-profile=cpu-bfloat16

is an unseeded CPU sweep, without the strict profile baseline. See TESTING.md for focused checks and baseline maintenance.

CUDA support and measurement limits:

Kornia accepts CUDA tensors for GPU acceleration, subject to each operator's dtype and backend limitations. There is no blocking CUDA CI job or checked-in CUDA known-failure manifest, so the CPU xfail counts above do not provide a current CUDA pass rate. The previous local measurements are retained here as historical evidence only:

Historical run (, 2026-09-23)

These used an RTX 4090, Python 3.11 and PyTorch 2.14.0+cu130. Source-marked xfails were excluded. Half tests ran in-process with KORNIA_TEST_IN_SUBPROCESS=1, followed by isolated retries of failures; two homography tests were deselected. They are not a measurement of the current branch. Those two tests (TestFindHomographyDLT::test_nocrash and ) now pass locally in all three CUDA dtypes at ; a fresh full CUDA sweep is needed before quoting new totals.

For CUDA half tests, use so each test gets a fresh process. They are skipped by default without it; selecting a half dtype alone does not exercise CUDA half support:

pixi run test-module tests/color/ --device=cuda --dtype=float16,bfloat16 --isolate-half-precision

Kornia is an open-source project that is developed and maintained by volunteers. Whether you're using it for research or commercial purposes, consider sponsoring or collaborating with us. Your support will help ensure Kornia's growth and ongoing innovation. Reach out to us today and be a part of shaping the future of this exciting initiative!

Some features (ONNX, Stable Diffusion dissolving) need extra packages; see Optional extras.

Kornia is not just another computer vision library — it's your gateway to effortless Computer Vision and AI.

If kornia is useful to you and you would like to help, contributions of many kinds are welcome: code, bug reports, benchmarks, documentation, questions, answers, and examples. The maintainers have limited time, so we cannot promise that every proposal or pull request will be reviewed or merged.

Strengthen the Core (Priority)

Kornia's differentiated value is its geometry core: warping and sampling, homographies, cameras, epipolar geometry, rotations and Lie groups, and geometry-consistent augmentation. The highest-impact contributions make that core more trustworthy — see the Roadmap for the full picture. Great entry points:

  • Benchmark results from your hardware: run the benchmark suite with and send the JSON — CUDA numbers from diverse GPUs are especially useful.
  • Convention pinning tests and conformance vectors for core geometry operations.
  • Corrective error messages: upgrade bare shape assertions into errors that state what was wrong, what was expected, and which convention applies.
  • Classical vision in the core domain: camera intrinsic calibration, fiducial markers (ArUco/ChArUco), classical tracking, dense stereo, and Hough transforms. An early design discussion can be useful for work of this size.

The model zoo is currently while maintainer bandwidth concentrates on the core. Shipped models (LoFTR, LightGlue, DISK, DeDoDe, SAM, and friends) stay available and maintained, and model work approved before the freeze (Efficient LoFTR, SANDesc) will be completed under its existing scope. New integrations — including VLM/VLA models — require a named maintainer sponsor who accepts ongoing ownership of the integration; a contributor implementation alone cannot reopen the surface. See the Roadmap for the reasoning and the reopen condition.

Documentation And Tutorial Optimization

Kornia's foundation lies in its extensive collection of classic computer vision operators, providing robust tools for image processing, feature extraction, and geometric transformations. We continuously seek for contributors to help us improve our documentation and present nice tutorials to our users.

If you are using kornia in your research-related documents, it is recommended that you cite the paper. See more in CITATION.

@inproceedings{eriba2019kornia,
  author    = {E. Riba, D. Mishkin, D. Ponsa, E. Rublee and G. Bradski},
  title     = {Kornia: an Open Source Differentiable Computer Vision Library for PyTorch},
  booktitle = {Winter Conference on Applications of Computer Vision},
  year      = {2020},
  url       = {https://arxiv.org/pdf/1910.02190.pdf}
}
  • report bugs and propose concrete changes. Open an issue
  • ask questions and discuss implementations, research, and ideas. Join a discussion

Kornia is released under the Apache 2.0 license. See the LICENSE file for more information.

items.title: cjpais/Handy
items.content:
A free, open source, and extensible speech-to-text application that works completely offline.

A free, open source, and extensible speech-to-text application that works completely offline.

Handy is a cross-platform desktop application that provides simple, privacy-focused speech transcription. Press a shortcut, speak, and have your words appear in any text field. This happens on your own computer without sending any information to the cloud.

Handy was created to fill the gap for a truly open source, extensible speech-to-text tool. As stated on handy.computer:

  • : Accessibility tooling belongs in everyone's hands, not behind a paywall
  • : Together we can build further. Extend Handy for yourself and contribute to something bigger
  • : Your voice stays on your computer. Get transcriptions without sending audio to the cloud
  • : One tool, one job. Transcribe what you say and put it into a text box
  1. a configurable keyboard shortcut: hold it to record and release to stop, or tap it to toggle recording on and off (Hold-only and Toggle-only modes are also available)
  2. your words while the shortcut is active
  3. and Handy processes your speech using Whisper
  4. your transcribed text pasted directly into whatever app you're using

The process is entirely local:

  • Silence is filtered using VAD (Voice Activity Detection) with Silero
  • Transcription uses your choice of models:
    • (Small/Medium/Turbo/Large) with GPU acceleration when available
    • - CPU-optimized model with excellent performance and automatic language detection
  • Works on Windows, macOS, and Linux
  1. Download the latest release from the releases page or the website
    • : Also available via winget: winget install cjpais.Handy The Homebrew cask and winget package are not maintained by the Handy developers.
    • : Install the downloaded with APT so required dependencies are installed automatically:
      sudo apt install ./Handy_*.deb
      Do not use unless the dependencies are already installed. If you already used it, run sudo apt --fix-broken install.
  2. Launch Handy and grant necessary system permissions (microphone, accessibility)
  3. Configure your preferred keyboard shortcuts in Settings

For detailed build instructions including platform-specific requirements, see BUILD.md.

Control Handy from Raycast — start/stop recording, browse transcript history, manage dictionary, switch models and languages.

Handy includes an advanced debug mode for development and troubleshooting. Access it by pressing:

  • :

Handy supports command-line flags for controlling a running instance and customizing startup behavior. These work on all platforms (macOS, Windows, Linux). Largely this is a beta feature.

(sent to an already-running instance via the single-instance plugin):

handy --toggle-transcription    # Toggle recording on/off
handy --toggle-post-process     # Toggle recording with post-processing on/off
handy --cancel                  # Cancel the current operation

handy --start-hidden            # Start without showing the main window
handy --no-tray                 # Start without the system tray icon
handy --debug                   # Enable debug mode with verbose logging
handy --help                    # Show all available flags

Flags can be combined for autostart scenarios:

handy --start-hidden --no-tray

When Handy is installed as an app bundle, invoke the binary directly:

/Applications/Handy.app/Contents/MacOS/Handy --toggle-transcription

Known Issues & Current Limitations

This project is actively being developed and has some known issues. We believe in transparency about the current state:

Bluetooth Headset Microphones (macOS)

Using a Bluetooth headset microphone on macOS may temporarily reduce playback quality or volume while recording because Bluetooth switches to bidirectional audio. Keep your headphones as the output device and select your Mac's built-in or an external microphone in Handy to avoid this.

fn and Globe Key Shortcuts (macOS)

Shortcuts that include the (Globe) key only work on Apple keyboards — your Mac's built-in keyboard or an Apple external keyboard. They will never trigger on a third-party keyboard, even while it is connected to the same Mac.

This is a hardware limitation rather than a Handy bug. is not part of the standard USB HID keyboard specification: Apple reports it through a vendor-specific usage that macOS honors only from Apple devices, while third-party keyboards handle their key entirely in firmware and send nothing to the computer. There is no event for Handy to listen for.

If you switch between a MacBook keyboard and an external one, pick a shortcut built from standard modifiers (, , , ) or a regular key instead.

For reliable text input on Linux, install the appropriate tool for your display server:

(requires group)
  • : Install for both direct typing and clipboard paste shortcuts
  • : Has Wayland display server by default. does not work, you need to install and configure systemd as described here.
  • : Install (preferred) or for text input to work correctly
  • : Requires adding your user to the group: sudo usermod -aG input $USER (then log out and back in)

Without these tools, Handy falls back to enigo which may have limited compatibility, especially on Wayland.

  • Limited support for Wayland display server

  • Runtime library dependency ():

    • Handy links on Linux. If startup fails with error while loading shared libraries: libgtk-layer-shell.so.0, install the runtime package for your distro:

      sudo apt install libgtk-layer-shell0
      sudo dnf install gtk-layer-shell
      sudo pacman -S gtk-layer-shell

    • For building from source on Ubuntu/Debian, you may also need .

  • The recording overlay is disabled by default on Linux () because certain compositors treat it as the active window. When the overlay is visible it can steal focus, which prevents Handy from pasting back into the application that triggered transcription. If you enable the overlay anyway, be aware that clipboard-based pasting might fail or end up in the wrong window.

  • Global keyboard shortcuts (Wayland): On Wayland, system-level shortcuts must be configured through your desktop environment or window manager. Use the CLI flags as the command for your custom shortcut.

    1. Open Settings > Keyboard > Keyboard Shortcuts > Custom Shortcuts
    2. Click the button to add a new shortcut
    3. Set the to Toggle Handy Transcription
    4. Set the to handy --toggle-transcription
    5. Click and press your desired key combination (e.g., )
    1. Open System Settings > Shortcuts > Custom Shortcuts
    2. Click Edit > New > Global Shortcut > Command/URL
    3. Name it Toggle Handy Transcription
    4. In the tab, set your desired key combination
    5. In the tab, set the command to handy --toggle-transcription

    Add to your config file ( or ):

    bindsym $mod+o exec handy --toggle-transcription

    Add to your config file (~/.config/hypr/hyprland.conf):

    bind = $mainMod, O, exec, handy --toggle-transcription

  • You can also trigger Handy externally via Unix signals or the CLI flags, which lets Wayland window managers or other hotkey daemons keep ownership of keybindings:

    or handy --toggle-transcription
    Toggle transcription with post-processinghandy --toggle-post-process
    bindsym $mod+o exec pkill -USR2 -n handy
bindsym $mod+p exec handy --toggle-post-process

    here simply delivers the signal—it does not terminate the process.

    older releases also accepted for toggling transcription with post-processing. WebKitGTK — the webview engine embedded in Handy on Linux — uses SIGUSR1 internally to coordinate JavaScript garbage collection, so listening for it caused phantom recordings and interrupted dictations every few minutes (#1660). Handy no longer listens for SIGUSR1 on Linux; the post-processing toggle is still available via handy --toggle-post-process. Remove any bindings: the signal is now delivered straight to WebKit's internal handler and can crash the app.

Overlay & Pasting Issues (Linux):

  • The recording overlay window can interfere with pasting transcribed text into target applications on Linux (X11)
  • Open and set to to disable the overlay
  • Enable (also in Advanced) if you still want audible confirmation of recording state
  • Users who upgrade from older versions or import settings from other platforms may need to manually apply this change

Verify Release Signatures

Handy release artifacts are signed with Tauri's updater signature format. The public key is stored in src-tauri/tauri.conf.json under .

To verify a release manually, set to the filename you downloaded, save the value from src-tauri/tauri.conf.json to , then decode the public key and matching file from base64 and verify the artifact with :

# Replace with the file you downloaded
ARTIFACT="Handy_0.8.1_amd64.AppImage"

python3 - "$ARTIFACT" <<'PY'
import base64, pathlib, sys

artifact = sys.argv[1]

pub = pathlib.Path("handy.pub.b64").read_text().strip()
pathlib.Path("handy.pub").write_bytes(base64.b64decode(pub))

sig = pathlib.Path(f"{artifact}.sig").read_text().strip()
pathlib.Path(f"{artifact}.minisig").write_bytes(base64.b64decode(sig))
PY

minisign -Vm "$ARTIFACT" \
  -p handy.pub \
  -x "$ARTIFACT.minisig"

On success, prints:

Signature and comment signature verified

Do not use for these files.

Previous Clipboard Content Is Pasted Instead of the Transcription

If the transcription is correct in but Handy inserts text you copied earlier, see issue #502. With the standard clipboard paste method, Handy restores your previous clipboard after a fixed delay. Under load, the receiving application may read the clipboard only after that restoration.

  1. Open Handy's settings window and press (macOS) or (Windows/Linux) to reveal .
  2. On , try in Debug with a clipboard paste method selected. It uses clipboard read notifications to delay restoration instead of relying on the standard fixed delay. Test it in the application where the problem occurs; it is still experimental.
  3. If Reliable Paste is disabled or unavailable, increase in Debug and test again. This controls the wait before restoring your previous clipboard. controls the wait before sending the paste keystroke and addresses a different part of the operation. These delay settings apply to the standard paste path, not Reliable Paste.

If the problem persists, add your Handy version, operating system, receiving application, paste method, Reliable Paste setting, and before/after delays to the existing issue. Redact private dictated text before sharing logs.

Manual Model Installation (For Proxy Users or Network Restrictions)

If you're behind a proxy, firewall, or in a restricted network environment where Handy cannot download models automatically, you can manually download and install them. The URLs are publicly accessible from any browser.

Step 1: Find Your App Data Directory

  1. Navigate to the section
  2. Copy the "App Data Directory" path shown there, or use the shortcuts:
    • : to open debug menu
    • : to open debug menu
  • : ~/Library/Application Support/com.pais.handy/
  • : C:\Users\{username}\AppData\Roaming\com.pais.handy\
  • : ~/.config/com.pais.handy/

Step 2: Create Models Directory

Inside your app data directory, create a folder if it doesn't already exist:

# macOS/Linux
mkdir -p ~/Library/Application\ Support/com.pais.handy/models

# Windows (PowerShell)
New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force -Path "$env:APPDATA\com.pais.handy\models"

Step 3: Download Model Files

Download the models you want from below

Whisper Models (single .bin files):

  • Small (487 MB): https://blob.handy.computer/ggml-small.bin
  • Medium (492 MB): https://blob.handy.computer/whisper-medium-q4_1.bin
  • Turbo (1600 MB): https://blob.handy.computer/ggml-large-v3-turbo.bin
  • Large (1100 MB): https://blob.handy.computer/ggml-large-v3-q5_0.bin

Parakeet Unified EN 0.6B (single file, recommended):

  • Q8_0 (731 MB): https://huggingface.co/handy-computer/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b-gguf/resolve/main/parakeet-unified-en-0.6b-Q8_0.gguf

For Whisper Models (.bin files):

Simply place the file directly into the directory:

{app_data_dir}/models/
├── ggml-small.bin
├── whisper-medium-q4_1.bin
├── ggml-large-v3-turbo.bin
└── ggml-large-v3-q5_0.bin

For GGUF Models (.gguf files):

Place the file directly into the directory, exactly like the Whisper files above. Handy also picks up models already present in the shared Hugging Face cache (), so a copy downloaded by another tool works without being moved.

  • Do not rename the or files—use the exact filenames from the download URLs
  • After placing the files, restart Handy to detect the new models

Step 5: Verify Installation

  1. Your manually installed models should now appear as "Downloaded"
  2. Select the model you want to use and test transcription

Handy can auto-discover custom Whisper GGML models placed in the directory. This is useful for users who want to use fine-tuned or community models not included in the default model list.

  1. Obtain a Whisper model in GGML format (e.g., from Hugging Face)
  2. Place the file in your directory (see paths above)
  3. Restart Handy to discover the new model
  4. The model will appear in the "Custom Models" section of the Models settings page
  • Community models are user-provided and may not receive troubleshooting assistance
  • The model must be a valid Whisper GGML format ( file)
  • Model name is derived from the filename (e.g., → "My Custom Model")

Linux Startup Crashes or Instability

If Handy fails to start reliably on Linux — for example, it crashes shortly after launch, never shows its window, or reports a Wayland protocol error — try the steps below in order.

1. Install (or reinstall)

Handy uses for its recording overlay and links against it at runtime. A missing or broken installation is the most common cause of startup failures and can manifest as a crash or a hang well before any window is shown. Make sure the runtime package is installed for your distro:

sudo apt install libgtk-layer-shell0
sudo dnf install gtk-layer-shell
sudo pacman -S gtk-layer-shell

If it is already installed and you still see startup problems, try reinstalling it (e.g. sudo pacman -S gtk-layer-shell again) in case the library files were corrupted by a partial upgrade.

2. Disable the GTK layer shell overlay ()

If installing the library does not help, you can skip initialization entirely as a workaround. On some compositors (notably KDE Plasma under Wayland) it has been reported to interact poorly with the recording overlay. With this variable set, the overlay falls back to a regular always-on-top window:

HANDY_NO_GTK_LAYER_SHELL=1 handy

3. Configure WebKit DMA-BUF rendering (WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER)

Handy disables the WebKitGTK DMA-BUF renderer by default on Linux because it can cause blank windows or crashes on some GPU/driver combinations. Explicit environment-variable values are preserved, including in the Nix package. To explicitly keep the renderer disabled:

WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER=1 handy

Some users on WebKitGTK 2.54 report a flickering or partially drawn recording overlay with the renderer disabled (#2166). If affected, try opting out of the default workaround:

WEBKIT_DISABLE_DMABUF_RENDERER=0 handy

This allows WebKit to use the renderer when supported, but can reintroduce the GPU/driver-specific crashes described above. Remove the override or use if that happens.

Fully quit Handy, including its tray instance, before testing either value. Running a second instance with does not change the running process's environment.

Making a workaround permanent

Set the variable in the environment of the launcher that actually starts Handy. Shell profile exports may not apply to desktop-menu or autostart launches. If you launch Handy from a file, you can prefix the line, e.g.:

Exec=env HANDY_NO_GTK_LAYER_SHELL=1 handy

Handy's built-in autostart rewrites its generated desktop entry, so editing that entry is not a durable workaround. For autostart, use an appropriate session/service environment, or disable Handy's built-in autostart and manage your own startup entry with the required variable.

If a workaround helps you, please open an issue describing your distro, desktop environment, and session type — that information helps us narrow down the underlying bug.

Empty recording overlay on Hyprland / Omarchy

If the recording overlay is empty or bordered, fully quit Handy and launch a native installation with Wayland enabled:

env -u HANDY_NO_GTK_LAYER_SHELL GDK_BACKEND=wayland handy

If this works, apply only to Handy's launcher. This workaround does not work with the 0.9.6 AppImage, which forces X11.

Vulkan Overlays and Capture Tools on Windows (HANDY_KEEP_VULKAN_IMPLICIT_LAYERS)

On Windows, Handy asks the Vulkan loader to skip implicit layers to avoid crashes caused by overlay and capture hooks (#2049). GPU acceleration remains enabled; this does not change system-wide settings.

To opt out for GPU selection or debugging tools, fully quit Handy (including the tray icon), then run both commands in the same PowerShell window:

$env:HANDY_KEEP_VULKAN_IMPLICIT_LAYERS = "1"
& "$env:ProgramFiles\Handy\handy.exe"

Adjust the executable path if needed. This override only applies to apps launched from that PowerShell session, not the Start menu. Handy also preserves any existing value.

The goal is to create both a useful tool and a foundation for others to build upon—a well-patterned, simple codebase that serves the community.

MIT License - see LICENSE file for details.

Handy is open-source software, but the Handy name, logo, icon, and brand assets are not open-source. Unofficial forks, rewrites, and redistributions must use their own branding and must not imply endorsement or affiliation.

  • by OpenAI for the speech recognition model
  • for an amazing cross-platform tensor library
  • for great lightweight VAD
  • team for the excellent Rust-based app framework
  • helping make Handy better

items.title: vorssaint/vorssaint-utils
items.content:
Free and open-source macOS menu bar toolkit.

One menu bar icon doing the job of a dozen paid Mac apps. Install only what you use.

Help keep Vorssaint free and open source. Share your product with Mac users.

Per app volume, a real system monitor, a better app switcher, window snapping, Dock previews, clipboard history, text snippets, a file shelf, an uninstaller. The utilities Mac users usually buy one by one, together behind a single menu bar icon, with no account, no telemetry and no subscription.

Install only what you use

Choose individual features or start with a preset. Uninstalled features stop loading and disappear from the interface; reinstalling restores their settings. Setup asks only for the permissions your choices need.

Reorder or hide panel sections, choose a compact layout, and export settings to another Mac. The app supports more than a dozen languages.

  • Set volume per app, boost quiet audio past 100%, and pin or reorder favorites. No audio driver required.
  • Play music through speakers while a call uses your headset.
  • Switch audio outputs with a shortcut and lower the volume when headphones disconnect.
  • Choose a preferred input, adjust its level on supported devices, and apply available microphone mute or input-volume controls with one shortcut. Siri and some apps may still hear you; Mic Mute is not a privacy lock. Its indicator shows that the feature is on, not that every app receives silence.
  • Prevent unwanted Music launches after detected playback-button presses. Requires Accessibility.

Know what your Mac is doing

  • CPU, GPU, memory, temperatures, battery health and power use, with history graphs and a view of energy-hungry apps.
  • Set manual fan speeds or temperature curves and monitor live RPM.
  • Put your chosen readings, usage bars, battery time or fan speed directly in the menu bar.
  • See live traffic, session totals and your local IP address, or run a speed test.
  • Get notified about sustained CPU load, high temperatures, memory pressure, low disk space or low battery.
  • Switch between apps and windows with live previews, search and display filters. A simpler mode works without screen capture.
  • Snap windows into layouts, move them between displays and restore earlier positions using shortcuts, screen edges or modifier-drag gestures.
  • Hover over Dock icons to preview windows across desktops. Switch, close, move or snap them from the preview.
  • Click an active app's Dock icon to minimize, hide or cycle through its windows.
  • Use the green button to fill the screen without creating another Space.
  • Keep Spaces in the order you set instead of rearranging them by recent use. Turning it off restores your previous setting.
  • Quit selected apps when their last window closes.
  • Quit and close protection. Prevent accidental ⌘Q or ⌘W with a hold, double press or extra modifier, per app.
  • Expand short triggers into text with clipboard, date and time variables, or insert snippets from a searchable menu.
  • Give your mouse wheel a fluid glide with adjustable speed and response.
  • Disable mouse acceleration and restore your previous setting when turned off.
  • Make every mouse wheel notch scroll the same number of lines, however fast the wheel spins.
  • Bring the window under the pointer forward after an adjustable pause.
  • Invert vertical and horizontal mouse scrolling independently of the trackpad.
  • Scroll sideways while holding a key. Turn vertical wheel movement into horizontal scrolling while holding a chosen key.
  • Use mouse Back and Forward buttons in Finder, browsers and compatible apps.
  • Assign keys to extra buttons and side wheels, or use button-drag gestures for Spaces and Mission Control.
  • Turn a three-finger trackpad press into a middle click.
  • Exclude chosen apps from mouse enhancements.
  • Ignore accidental rapid clicks from worn mouse buttons without delaying normal clicks.
  • Filter repeated letters caused by a worn keyboard.
  • Use Caps Lock or a right-side modifier as a shortcut combination, with a separate tap action and app exclusions.
  • Manage feature shortcuts in one place, including optional takeover of supported macOS shortcuts while a feature is active.

Clipboard, files and links

  • Search local text, image and file history, pin favorites, preview entries and paste with shortcuts.
  • Clear the system clipboard after a delay, sleep or lock, while keeping saved history.
  • Paste without formatting while preserving the original clipboard content.
  • Park files, text and links near your cursor while dragging, then drop or share them later.
  • Move files with ⌘X and ⌘V, rename with F2, or paste copied images as PNG files.
  • Remove tracking parameters from links, manually or automatically.
  • Install an app from a mounted disk image and eject it, with optional download cleanup.
  • Keep music, notifications, calendars, timers, downloads and everyday controls around the camera cutout, or a simulated one on other Macs. Customize sections and shortcuts, with optional lyrics, a live equalizer, camera preview and file tools.
  • Follow Claude, Codex, OpenCode and GitHub Copilot in the Dynamic Island: plan limits and when they reset where available, tokens, API value, models, projects and live work, with a notice when a long task finishes. Codex's banked resets can be used from there too, and each extra Codex account () can have a limits card of its own. Copilot uses local CLI/app session logs; its token totals update when shutdown metrics arrive, and aggregate API-value estimates use base rates.
  • Search apps, windows, files, clipboard history, snippets and app menu commands from one field. Calculate, convert units, find emoji or run saved scripts.
  • Open a floating palette of favorite tools with ⌃⌘V.
  • Switch appearance, hide desktop icons, eject disks, empty the Trash, lock the screen and more.
  • See every open app in one list and quit them one by one, all at once or all but the one in front.
  • Open a customizable wheel of apps, files, shortcuts and tools around the pointer, with profiles and submenus.
  • Keep autosaved notes in tabs, with Markdown preview and export, in a floating window or Dynamic Island.
  • Lock keyboard input while cleaning, with a black screen or a small visible indicator.
  • Switch between screenshots, recording, text recognition and color picking in one selector with a pixel magnifier.
  • Capture an area, window, screen or scrolling page. Annotate, crop, redact, add backgrounds and watermarks, pin captures, send them through the Share menu or share an expiring link.
  • Record with separate system-audio and microphone tracks. Trim, cut, add automatic zooms, blur private details and export video or GIFs, or share an expiring link.
  • Check your camera in a floating mirror or Dynamic Island before a call.
  • Recognize text offline from any screen area, or read a QR code.
  • Copy a screen color as HEX, RGB, HSL or SwiftUI code.
  • Compress and edit videos, batch-convert images, add watermarks, make GIFs and extract text, all locally.
  • Check store apps, package-managed apps and supported developer feeds in one list. Install managed updates together or open an app's own updater.
  • Remove caches, logs and app leftovers, manually or on a schedule.
  • Review, organize or move messaging downloads to the Trash using retention rules.
  • Remove apps and review their related caches, preferences and helpers before moving them to the Trash.
  • Search, install and remove formulae and casks without opening a terminal.
  • Find processes listening on network ports and stop them with Kill Process when installed.
  • Keep your Mac working on a timer, with the lid closed, or while selected apps, power or external displays are present.
  • Control individual displays and brightness, with hardware control where supported, half or quarter steps for the brightness keys, optional extra dimming below a monitor's minimum, and software dimming as a fallback.
  • Use a MacBook Pro XDR display's HDR headroom to go beyond its normal maximum brightness.
  • Disconnect Bluetooth during sleep and restore it on wake only if Vorssaint turned it off.
brew install --cask vorssaint

Or grab the disk image from the releases page and drag Vorssaint into Applications.

Builds are signed with an Apple Developer ID and notarized, so macOS opens them without a fuss and your permissions survive updates.

brew uninstall --cask vorssaint

To remove Vorssaint completely, including its settings and permissions:

Vorssaint is local-first, with no account, analytics or tracking. The network is touched only by things you can see: update checks, the speed test, Homebrew actions, optional online lyric lookup, temporary screenshot or recording links and feedback you explicitly send. The full story is in the privacy notes.

Permissions get the same treatment. Every one is optional, the app explains each in plain words, shows which features actually use it, and even tells you when a permission you granted is no longer needed by anything, with a shortcut to revoke it.

See the permissions guide for which features need access and what remains available without it.

    git clone https://github.com/vorssaint/vorssaint-utils.git
cd vorssaint-utils
./build.sh --dev            # build the separate Developer variant
./build.sh --dev --install  # install and launch it

    Xcode Command Line Tools are the only requirement. The contributing guide covers the layout and conventions. Official builds come only from the maintainer: the GPL covers the source, while the Vorssaint name, icon and look are covered by TRADEMARKS.md, so forks need their own identity.

    When something misbehaves

    Vorssaint went from first commit to the front of GitHub trending in three days, top of the Swift charts, and issues and pull requests have shaped every release since. Bug reports, feature ideas and translations are all welcome, starting from the contributing guide.

    Vorssaint is free and will stay that way. If it earned its place in your menu bar, a star helps other people find it, and a coffee keeps the maintainer awake, with or without the Keep awake feature.

    GPL 3.0 or later, copyright 2026 Vorssaint. The license covers the source code; the Vorssaint name, logo and look are covered separately in TRADEMARKS.md.
