items.title: Orkas-AI/Orkas
items.content:
Orkas is an open-source (MIT), local-first AI team for your desktop: a Commander turns your goal into to-dos and coordinates 16 built-in specialist agents plus Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, OpenClaw and Hermes, with projects, scheduled automations and connectors. Free app for macOS & Windows; built-in models or your own keys.

An open-source team of AI agents on your desktop — it turns your goals into finished work and keeps it moving.

Orkas is an open-source (MIT), local-first multi-agent desktop app — an AI assistant that works as a team. Tell the what you need: it finishes many tasks on its own, and for bigger work it plans the steps and brings in specialist agents along with the coding and personal agents you already use — Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, OpenClaw and Hermes-Agent — to work on it together.

Orkas is built to keep a project moving, not just answer one prompt. A holds the goal, rules, memory and files, so every new conversation picks up where the last one left off. split the work between people and agents, lets the team take on the next to-do by itself, and repeat routine work hourly, daily, weekly or monthly. All your data stays on your computer, and finished work comes back for your review — so you can trust Orkas with the ongoing work of your business.

— free, with 500 credits for the built-in Orkas model, so you don't need an API key to start. Prefer your own keys? Claude · OpenAI · Gemini · DeepSeek · Kimi · GLM · Qwen · MiniMax · Doubao, or a local OpenAI-compatible endpoint.

  • Videos, voice-overs and images — VideoStudio, VoiceStudio, ImageStudio
  • Research reports, SEO audits and market analysis — DeepResearcher, SeoGeoAgent, StockAnalyser
  • Posts, articles, newsletters and slide decks — ContentWriter, PptMaker
  • — UIDesigner, ProductDeveloper
  • Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF files — OfficeWorker
  • — product research, listings, review analysis, sales analysis and catalog changes, from five e-commerce agents
  • Complex work that takes several agents — the Commander splits it up, hands each part to the right agent and combines the results; for example, market research that becomes a report, a slide deck and a launch video

16 specialists ship with the app, each with its own skills, memory and tools. Browse 30+ agents in the agent marketplace, or describe the role you need and the Commander builds a custom agent for you.

Recreate a reference video with your own content

can recreate a viral video's narrative structure, visual style and editing pace using your own product, script and footage. Supply a reference video file and your assets: the agent analyzes the hook, information order, visual beats and call to action, then proposes what to preserve and what to replace before production.

This works best for motion-graphic explainers, SaaS or app demos, and product ads built from your existing footage. Locally authored text, captions, narration and clips can be revised separately; text baked into AI-generated footage requires changing that footage.

"Use reference.mp4 as a reference for a 30-second vertical promo. Keep its hook, typography and pacing, replace the content with my product and screen recordings, and show me the breakdown and plan first."

Start with a video file the agent can read; social-platform share-link downloading is not built in. Exact camera moves, human performances and frame-by-frame matching are not guaranteed. See the reference-recreation workflow.

One task is a good start. Orkas is built for the work that keeps going.

  • — goals & rules, memory and files that every conversation in the project starts from, so you never brief from scratch.
  • — every project has a to-do list for people and agents; with Auto-advance on, the team picks up the next item on its own and brings finished work back for your review.
  • — run any task hourly, daily, weekly or monthly. Orkas runs on your computer. From v1.9, each automation catches up its most recent missed run within 12 hours when the computer wakes or Orkas starts.
  • — Gmail, Google Calendar, Sheets and Drive, Notion, Slack, Shopify, Stripe and many more. By default, Orkas asks before it sends, posts or deletes anything.
  • — describe a tool and Orkas builds it as a local app inside the desktop app. In the packaged app, paid plans can also publish it as a web app with a public link.
  • — invite a teammate or VA, and give each to-do to a person or an agent.

Shared projects, cloud sync and web-app publishing are only in the packaged app — the open-source build doesn't support them yet. To use them, (free, with 500 credits to start).

Voice input also works in the source build. Configure an in , then click the microphone beside a composer. Allow microphone access when prompted. Audio is sent to Orkas for recognition and uses the key owner’s Orkas credits. Click again to stop, review the text, and send it yourself. If access was denied, enable the microphone in your system settings.

Run Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, OpenClaw and Hermes-Agent together

Orkas runs the CLI agents you already have installed as local sessions, next to its own specialists — the coding agents Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, and the personal agents OpenClaw and Hermes-Agent. The Commander hands each one the part it's best at and keeps one plan across all of them, so a single chat can fix the bug, review the change and draft the release note. Open-source tools such as HyperFrames plug in the same way.

  • A Commander that plans, delegates and does the rest — it breaks down goals, picks the right agents, skills, connectors and tools, and handles analysis, writing, research and file work itself when no specialist is a better fit.
  • — conversations, files, knowledge bases and custom agents stay on your disk by default. Cloud sync is optional in the packaged app. With your own keys, model calls go straight from your machine to the provider; the built-in Orkas model runs through Orkas's managed model service.
  • Any model, switch any time — the Commander and built-in agents share one model setting: the built-in Orkas model, your own provider, or a local endpoint. External CLI agents keep their own model settings.
  • — each agent keeps private skills and memory. Background reviews examine new activity when the app is idle and can refine self-assessment, reusable methods and learned skills.
  • Open source, no black box — MIT licensed. Read exactly what Orkas and every agent and skill do.

⭐ If Orkas is useful to you, a star helps more people find the project.

Packaged app (recommended)
macOS 12+ (Apple Silicon & Intel), Windows 10+macOS, Windows, glibc 2.34+ Linux x64/arm64
Sign in — 500 free credits
Built-in Orkas model, or your own keysYour own keys or a local endpoint
Project collaboration, app publishing, cloud sync, and more

The download link detects your system and starts the right installer.

  • — launch videos, product pages, posts and newsletters in your voice. Content writing · Videos
  • — weekly sales briefs, review replies, listings and competitor checks. E-commerce
  • — answers grounded in your own files, with citations back to the source passages. Chat with documents
  • — landing pages, bug fixes with tests, changelogs and launch posts. Developers
  • — quote calculators, booking forms, internal tools. Build apps
  • — one project for people and agents. Small teams
Anthropic's agentic coding tool — in the terminal, IDE, desktop and web, built on Claude models.Not either-or: Orkas runs Claude Code as one of its agents. Around it, Orkas adds a model-agnostic team for the work beyond code — research, content, video and more — with projects, to-dos and automations that keep it moving. Orkas vs Claude Code →
OpenAI's coding agent — in the terminal, your editor and the cloud.Not either-or: Orkas runs Codex as one of its agents, next to Claude Code and OpenCode. The Commander can hand the coding to Codex and the review to another agent, then cover the non-code half of a release — docs, launch posts and videos. Orkas vs Codex →
A developer framework/library for building LLM apps and agents — code-first, embedded in your own Python/JS app.Orkas is a desktop app you direct through chat, not by writing orchestration code. Data stays local by default.
A Python framework for orchestrating role-playing autonomous agents — you define crews and agents in code.Orkas brings multi-agent orchestration into a desktop app, with projects, to-dos, automations and per-agent self-improvement built in.
A personal-agent platform with messaging integrations, multi-agent routing and sub-agents.Orkas provides a desktop workspace for finished deliverables, with built-in specialists and coordination across Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and other CLI agents. OpenClaw can join that workflow as a CLI agent.
Nous Research's self-improving agent — one agent with memory and skills, available as a CLI, a messaging gateway and a desktop app.Orkas coordinates a team: the Commander directs many specialists and other CLI agents, and Hermes-Agent plugs in as one of them.

you want a team of agents rather than one assistant, work that keeps moving across days, and your data, keys and agents on your own disk.

you just want a single all-purpose chatbot, or a pure code library to embed in your own app.

Want a packaged installer instead? See Download above. To run from source — currently the way to run Orkas on Linux:

: Node 22.12+ · macOS / Windows 10+ / glibc 2.34+ Linux x64 or arm64. Keep Python 3 and a C/C++ build toolchain available for the uncommon native-module source-build fallback.

git clone https://github.com/Orkas-AI/Orkas.git
cd Orkas
./run.sh           # macOS / Linux
run.cmd            # Windows

Linux source runs require glibc 2.34+. Alpine and other musl-based distributions are not supported. Local speech transcription downloads and verifies the target-native whisper.cpp runtime and multilingual model during the first source launch.

/ installs the locked npm dependency tree and prepares the pinned Python, uv, Node, embedding model (~95 MB), OfficeCLI, FFmpeg, whisper.cpp, and multilingual speech model resources on first launch. Linux startup then verifies the platform-native modules and Whisper runtime under Electron's ABI before opening the app. OCR and Skill-specific Python packages are installed into isolated local environments when those features are first used. First launch creates a workspace under (macOS / Linux) or <smallest non-system drive>:\.orkas\ (Windows). Then open to add an API key or OAuth.

Native dependency errors: use Node.js 24 LTS (minimum 22.12.0), then run from this checkout. This restores optional packages, repairs SQLite for Electron, prepares bundled Node for isolated image processing, and checks SQL, sqlite-vec and sharp before success. Use for a check without installation. See the native dependency verification script for the checks performed.

The Commander handles general work itself and delegates specialist work through three tools:

  • runs a named agent and returns its result for continued work. It can wait for the result or run asynchronously and notify the Commander when the task finishes.
  • transfers the remaining work to a named agent and ends the current Commander turn. The agent delivers its own reply; an optional continuation lets the Commander resume a broader task afterward.
  • runs an anonymous, isolated sub-task and returns a private result. It does not receive conversation history or a named agent's skills.

The runtime budgets context against the selected model's usable input capacity, accounting for prompts, tools and persistent runtime state. Completed dialogue uses a bounded recent-history window; long active tasks use checkpoints to condense earlier process messages while retaining recent work. File reads, file changes and command executions also have structured records that can survive context compaction.

Durable notes keep user preferences, project facts and each agent's reusable knowledge in separate scopes. These notes are distinct from the Library's document index and the stored conversation history.

The Library extracts documents into passages and stores a local SQLite vector index. Its embedding model runs on your machine; the tool can list files, search relevant passages and read source content from the global or current-project Library. Earlier conversations are retrieved separately through .

Execution limits and recovery

Session locks and concurrency limits bound parallel work. Tool-round budgets, progress checkpoints, repeated-call checks and phase-aware idle watchdogs help contain runs that stall or repeat work. Named agent tasks can be tracked and cancelled individually; an admitted or queued task is not treated as a completed result.

Background reviews examine new agent activity when the app is idle, subject to cooldowns and execution limits. A review may update an agent's self-assessment (), reusable methods () or learned skills. Reviews depend on new activity rather than task count, and can conclude that there is nothing worth saving.

Orkas is an open-source (MIT), local-first multi-agent desktop app. Its Commander turns your goal into to-dos and coordinates 16 built-in specialist agents — plus Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, OpenClaw and Hermes-Agent — to deliver finished files. Not a single chatbot, not a code framework, not a hosted SaaS.

No. The packaged app comes with 500 credits for the built-in Orkas model. After that, buy credits, choose a paid plan or add your own provider keys; provider charges are separate.

No. Orkas runs on your machine and calls the models you choose — the built-in Orkas model, your own API keys, or a local model endpoint. It orchestrates agents and tools; it is not itself a model.

Can Orkas answer questions from my documents, with citations? Yes. Add PDFs and documents to your local Library; Orkas can search them and answer with citations to source passages, so you can open the original and check. The index is built on your machine.

Can I use local models like Ollama or LM Studio? Yes. Open Account settings → Models → Chat → Add model → Custom, select or , and enter the base URL, exact model ID, and API key. Choose the saved model from the task's model control.

Where are my API keys and data stored? On your disk by default. Your own provider keys are encrypted locally and excluded from cloud sync. With your own keys, model calls go straight from your machine to the provider; the built-in Orkas model uses Orkas's managed service. Optional cloud sync and shared projects in the packaged app store the selected data on Orkas servers. Security and data handling →

The source build can run fully offline against a local model endpoint. The packaged app needs to sign in, and cloud models need a network connection.

Does it keep working when my computer is off? No — Orkas runs on your computer, so Auto-advance and automations need the computer awake and Orkas running. From v1.9, each automation catches up its most recent missed run within 12 hours when the computer wakes or Orkas starts.

Can I build and publish apps? Yes. Local apps that run inside Orkas are free. Publishing a web app to a public link needs a paid plan (Lite 5, Pro 8, Max 15 apps), and published web apps don't include every capability available inside Orkas.

Do I need an Orkas account? The packaged desktop app asks you to sign in when you first launch it. The source build in this repository has no account layer at all — it boots straight into the app.

Can Orkas drive Claude Code and other CLI agents? Yes. Orkas can drive five external CLI agents as local subprocesses — the coding agents Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, plus the personal agents OpenClaw and Hermes-Agent — and onboard open-source projects like HyperFrames, all directed from the same chat.

How is Orkas different from Claude Code / Codex / CrewAI / LangChain? Claude Code and Codex are coding agents — Orkas runs both as members of its team, so you don't have to choose between them; CrewAI and LangChain are code-first frameworks. Orkas is an open-source desktop app where a Commander coordinates a team of specialist agents and your CLI agents, with any model provider, and keeps data and keys local. See the full comparisons.

Which platforms does Orkas support? macOS 12+ (Apple Silicon and Intel) and Windows 10+ have packaged installers. glibc 2.34+ Linux x64/arm64 runs from source today, with no installer yet. Local speech transcription is supported on Linux through the pinned whisper.cpp runtime prepared on first launch. Alpine and other musl-based distributions are not supported. The source bootstrap needs Node 22.12+; Python 3 and a C/C++ build toolchain are needed only when a native npm package has no compatible prebuilt binary and must be rebuilt locally.

Is Orkas free and open source? Yes — the app is MIT licensed and free to use. The packaged app includes 500 credits for the built-in Orkas model; paid plans from $11.99/month add monthly credits, cloud sync, more shared projects and app publishing. With your own keys, model usage is billed by your provider; Orkas does not add a markup. Pricing →

items.title: lightpanda-io/browser
items.content:
Lightpanda: the headless browser designed for AI and automation

The headless browser built from scratch for AI agents and automation. Not a Chromium fork. Not a WebKit patch. A new browser, written in Zig.

16x lighter and 9x faster than Chromium.

Requesting 933 real web pages over the network on a AWS EC2 m5.large instance. See benchmark details.

Execution time (100 pages)

Latest nightly from Homebrew:

brew install lightpanda-io/browser/lightpanda

Latest nightly from Arch Linux User Repository:

yay -S lightpanda-nightly-bin

Download from the nightly builds

You can download the last binary from the nightly builds for Linux and MacOS for both x86_64 and aarch64.

curl -L -o lightpanda https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/releases/download/nightly/lightpanda-x86_64-linux && \
chmod a+x ./lightpanda

Verify the binary before running anything:

If you use , you can run Lightpanda directly from the flake without downloading a binary:

nix run github:lightpanda-io/browser -- --help

Or pin it as an input in your own flake:

{
  inputs.lightpanda.url = "github:lightpanda-io/browser";
}

The Linux release binaries are linked against glibc. On musl-based Linux distributions (Alpine, etc.) the binary fails with cannot execute: required file not found because the glibc dynamic linker is missing. Use a glibc-based base image: the current release binaries need glibc () or (), so (2.36) is fine on but too old for — use , , or there — or build from sources.

there is no native Android build. The Linux aarch64 binary needs the glibc loader (/lib/ld-linux-aarch64.so.1), which Android's Bionic libc does not provide, so it fails with the same cannot execute: required file not found error.

curl -L -o lightpanda https://github.com/lightpanda-io/browser/releases/download/nightly/lightpanda-aarch64-macos && \
chmod a+x ./lightpanda

Lightpanda has no native Windows binary. Install it inside WSL following the Linux steps above.

Your automation client (Puppeteer, Playwright, etc.) can run either inside WSL or on the Windows host. WSL forwards automatically.

Lightpanda provides official Docker images for both Linux amd64 and arm64 architectures. The following command fetches the Docker image and starts a new container exposing Lightpanda's CDP server on port .

docker run -d --name lightpanda -p 127.0.0.1:9222:9222 lightpanda/browser:latest

./lightpanda fetch --obey-robots --dump html --log-format pretty  --log-level info https://demo-browser.lightpanda.io/campfire-commerce/

You can use to convert directly into markdown, or or for a text-only rendering of the page. prints the page's JSON-LD, OpenGraph, Twitter card, meta and link tags as JSON, like the MCP tool. , , and are available to adjust waiting time before dump.

./lightpanda serve --obey-robots --log-format pretty  --log-level info --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9222

To listen on a Unix-domain socket (owner-only, mode 0600) instead of TCP:

./lightpanda serve --unix-socket /run/user/1000/lightpanda.sock

Once the CDP server started, you can run a Puppeteer script by configuring the .

Start a webdriver Bidi server

Use to enable Bidi support. You can start both, CDP and Bidi, with --protocol webdriver --protocol cdp

./lightpanda serve --obey-robots --log-format pretty  --log-level info --host 127.0.0.1 --port 9222 --protocol webdriver

lets you drive the browser with a native agent. Describe what you want in plain English or with slash commands, and it controls the browser: navigating pages, clicking through flows, filling forms, extracting structured data. Think of it as a robot you're directing to use the web, more than a chatbot you're having a conversation with.

Because the agent runs inside the same process as the browser, every tool call is a direct operation and you retain Lightpanda's speed and memory advantage.

The output of an agent session is a PandaScript: vanilla JavaScript with a small set of native browser primitives built directly into Lightpanda. Run to export one from your current session, then replay it with lightpanda run <script>.js. Scripts are deterministic and token-free, so you can prototype with the LLM and ship the output to production without a model at runtime.

It supports Anthropic, OpenAI, Gemini, Google Vertex AI, Mistral, Hugging Face, the multi-lab gateways Vercel AI Gateway and OpenRouter (one key for hundreds of models), any OpenAI-compatible endpoint via , and local models via Ollama, llama.cpp or LLMD. You can also run without an LLM using , which drops you into the REPL. See the agent documentation for the full reference.

./lightpanda agent                                    # auto-detects API key from env
./lightpanda agent --task "top story on news.ycombinator.com?"
./lightpanda agent --no-llm                           # basic REPL, no LLM
./lightpanda run session.js                           # run a recorded script
cat session.js | ./lightpanda run -                   # ...or pipe one in via stdin
./lightpanda agent --provider gemini --task "..."     # force a specific provider
./lightpanda agent --list-models                      # models available for the detected provider
VERTEX_API_KEY=... ./lightpanda agent --provider vertex             # Vertex AI, express mode
GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT=my-proj ./lightpanda agent --provider vertex   # Vertex AI, token via gcloud auth
AI_GATEWAY_API_KEY=... ./lightpanda agent --provider vercel --model moonshotai/kimi-k2   # any model behind Vercel AI Gateway
OPENROUTER_API_KEY=... ./lightpanda agent --provider openrouter --model anthropic/claude-sonnet-5   # any model behind OpenRouter
OPENAI_BASE_URL=https://my-gateway/v1 OPENAI_API_KEY=... ./lightpanda agent            # any OpenAI-compatible server

The MCP server communicates via MCP JSON-RPC 2.0 over stdio.

Add to your MCP configuration:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "lightpanda": {
      "command": "/path/to/lightpanda",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}

HTTP transport and independent sessions

For serving several agents from one process, start the MCP server over HTTP instead of stdio by giving it a port (add to specify the interface to listen on):

lightpanda mcp --port 9223

Clients POST JSON-RPC to . Each connection is routed to its own — its own page, cookies and memory — so agents no longer clobber each other's page:

  • A client that s without an header is assigned a fresh session; the id comes back in the response's header. Send it on subsequent requests to stay on that session ().
  • Two agents that send the share one browsing context ( — e.g. a workflow where several agents work the same page).
  • The , and tools manage sessions explicitly. Sending with an closes that session.

The tool runs a PandaScript in the caller's session, as does, and returns its console output and the value it returns. It takes the source as , or the of a file that wrote. Pages the script opens are closed when it ends; cookies and storage stay, so a login carries over to the next . An optional in milliseconds (default 60000) stops a stuck script. A backend can drive Lightpanda with one POST:

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:9223/mcp -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "jsonrpc": "2.0", "id": 1, "method": "tools/call",
  "params": { "name": "run", "arguments": { "script":
    "const page = new Page();\nawait page.goto(\"https://example.com\");\nreturn page.extract({ title: \"title\", links: [\"a\"] });" } }
}'

lightpanda completion <bash | fish | zsh> prints a completion script for commands, flags and their values:

lightpanda completion fish > ~/.config/fish/completions/lightpanda.fish
lightpanda completion bash > ~/.local/share/bash-completion/completions/lightpanda
lightpanda completion zsh > ~/.zfunc/_lightpanda  # with fpath=(~/.zfunc $fpath) before compinit

By default, Lightpanda collects and sends usage telemetry. This can be disabled by setting an environment variable LIGHTPANDA_DISABLE_TELEMETRY=true. You can read Lightpanda's privacy policy at: https://lightpanda.io/privacy-policy.

Set LIGHTPANDA_DISABLE_CORE_DUMP (to any value) to suppress crash core dumps by zeroing the soft at startup.

Lightpanda is written with Zig. You have to install it with the right version in order to build the project.

To be able to build the v8 engine, you have to install some libs:

For Debian/Ubuntu based Linux:

sudo apt install xz-utils ca-certificates \
    pkg-config libglib2.0-dev \
    clang make curl git

For systems with , you can use the devShell.

For , you need cmake and Rust.

You can build the entire browser with or for debug env.

But you can directly use the zig command: .

Lighpanda uses v8 snapshot. By default, it is created on startup but you can embed it by using the following commands:

zig build snapshot_creator -- src/snapshot.bin

Build using the snapshot binary.

zig build -Dsnapshot_path=../../snapshot.bin

See #1279 for more details.

You can test Lightpanda by running .

make test                                       # Run all tests
make test F="server"                            # Filter by substring
TEST_FILTER="WebApi: #selector_all" make test   # Filter main + subtest (separator: #)
TEST_VERBOSE=true make test
TEST_FAIL_FIRST=true make test
METRICS=true make test                          # Capture allocation/duration metrics as JSON
TEST_JOBS=1 make test                           # Run in one process (default: up to 4, or 1 when filtered)

To run end to end tests, you need to clone the demo repository into dir.

You also need to install Go > v1.24.

For reference, you can execute a WPT test case with your browser via wpt.live.

Configure WPT HTTP server

To run the test, you must clone the repository, configure the custom hosts and generate the file.

Clone the repository with the branch.

git clone -b fork --depth=1 git@github.com:lightpanda-io/wpt.git

Install custom domains in your 

./wpt make-hosts-file | sudo tee -a /etc/hosts

First start the WPT's HTTP server from your clone dir.

zig build -Dwpt_extensions run -- serve \
    --ws-max-concurrent 64 \
    --insecure-disable-tls-host-verification \
    --load-resources iframe \
    --load-resources image \
    --load-resources worker \
    --load-resources stylesheet

Then you can start the wptrunner from the demo's clone dir:

cd wptrunner && go run . Node-childNodes.html

command accepts and options modifying output. Also define the concurrency limit.

To check a single test case without the runner, prints its results as JSON: the harness status, a pass/fail summary and the cases that did not pass. It relies on the fork's .

zig build -Dwpt_extensions run -- fetch \
    --insecure-disable-tls-host-verification \
    --load-resources worker \
    --load-resources iframe \
    --dump wpt \
    --wait-script "window.report && report.complete" \
    "http://web-platform.test:8000/dom/nodes/Node-childNodes.html"

⚠️ Running the whole test suite will take a long time. In this case, it's useful to build in mode to make tests faster.

zig build -Dwpt_extensions -Doptimize=fast run -- serve ...

Javascript execution is mandatory for the modern web

Simple HTTP requests used to be enough for web automation. That's no longer the case. Javascript now drives most of the web:

  • Ajax, Single Page Apps, infinite loading, instant search
  • JS frameworks: React, Vue, Angular, and others

Chrome is not the right tool

Running a full desktop browser on a server works, but it does not scale well. Chrome at hundreds or thousands of instances is expensive:

  • Hard to package, deploy, and maintain at scale
  • Many features are not necessary in headless made

Lightpanda is built for performance

Supporting Javascript with real performance meant building from scratch rather than forking Chromium:

  • Not based on Chromium, Blink, or WebKit
  • Written in Zig, a low-level language with explicit memory control
  • No graphical rendering engine

items.title: anthropics/skills
items.content:
Public repository for Agent Skills

This repository contains Anthropic's implementation of skills for Claude. For information about the Agent Skills standard, see agentskills.io.

Skills are folders of instructions, scripts, and resources that Claude loads dynamically to improve performance on specialized tasks. Skills teach Claude how to complete specific tasks in a repeatable way, whether that's creating documents with your company's brand guidelines, analyzing data using your organization's specific workflows, or automating personal tasks.

For more information, check out:

This repository contains skills that demonstrate what's possible with Claude's skills system. These skills range from creative applications (art, music, design) to technical tasks (testing web apps, MCP server generation) to enterprise workflows (communications, branding, etc.).

Each skill is self-contained in its own folder with a file containing the instructions and metadata that Claude uses. Browse through these skills to get inspiration for your own skills or to understand different patterns and approaches.

Many skills in this repo are open source (Apache 2.0). We've also included the document creation & editing skills that power Claude's document capabilities under the hood in the , , , and subfolders. These are source-available, not open source, but we wanted to share these with developers as a reference for more complex skills that are actively used in a production AI application.

These skills are provided for demonstration and educational purposes only. While some of these capabilities may be available in Claude, the implementations and behaviors you receive from Claude may differ from what is shown in these skills. These skills are meant to illustrate patterns and possibilities. Always test skills thoroughly in your own environment before relying on them for critical tasks.

  • ./skills: Skill examples for Creative & Design, Development & Technical, Enterprise & Communication, and Document Skills
  • ./spec: The Agent Skills specification

You can register this repository as a Claude Code Plugin marketplace by running the following command in Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add anthropics/skills

Then, to install a specific set of skills:

  1. Select Browse and install plugins
  2. Select
  3. Select or

Alternatively, directly install either Plugin via:

/plugin install document-skills@anthropic-agent-skills
/plugin install example-skills@anthropic-agent-skills

After installing the plugin, you can use the skill by just mentioning it. For instance, if you install the plugin from the marketplace, you can ask Claude Code to do something like: "Use the PDF skill to extract the form fields from "

These example skills are all already available to paid plans in Claude.ai.

To use any skill from this repository or upload custom skills, follow the instructions in Using skills in Claude.

You can use Anthropic's pre-built skills, and upload custom skills, via the Claude API. See the Skills API Quickstart for more.

Skills are simple to create - just a folder with a file containing YAML frontmatter and instructions. You can use the in this repository as a starting point:

---
name: my-skill-name
description: A clear description of what this skill does and when to use it
---

# My Skill Name

[Add your instructions here that Claude will follow when this skill is active]

## Examples
- Example usage 1
- Example usage 2

## Guidelines
- Guideline 1
- Guideline 2

The frontmatter requires only two fields:

  • - A unique identifier for your skill (lowercase, hyphens for spaces)
  • - A complete description of what the skill does and when to use it

The markdown content below contains the instructions, examples, and guidelines that Claude will follow. For more details, see How to create custom skills.

Skills are a great way to teach Claude how to get better at using specific pieces of software. As we see awesome example skills from partners, we may highlight some of them here:

items.title: pingdotgg/t3code
items.content:
Works with your subscriptions on Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Google Antigravity, and fx. If they're set up on your computer, T3 Code can control them.

"Wait, what are you selling me?"

Nothing. We built T3 Code because we wanted the best possible development experience with agents. We were inspired by existing solutions like the Codex desktop app, Conductor, Claude Desktop and Cursor Glass, but none met our bar.

We wanted something performant, remote-ready, and truly open. If we ever go the wrong direction, we want you to have everything you need to fork and build the editor that you want.

T3 Code currently supports Codex, Claude, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode, Antigravity, and fx. Install and authenticate at least one provider before use:

  • OpenCode: install OpenCode and run
  • Antigravity: enable it in Settings, then use and . No CLI is required.
  • fx: install fx and run on the machine running the T3 Code server (setup guide)
curl -fsSL https://t3.codes/install.sh | sh

On Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https://t3.codes/install.ps1 | iex

Then run to start the server and open the local web app. keeps it running in the background, moves to a newer release, and has the full reference.

To try it once without installing, run instead.

Install the latest version of the desktop app from GitHub Releases, or from your favorite package registry:

winget install T3Tools.T3Code

scoop install extras/t3code

brew install --cask t3-code

sudo apt install ./T3-Code-*.deb

yay -S t3code-nightly-bin

The AUR packaging is maintained in this repository under .

nix profile add github:NixOS/nixpkgs/nixos-unstable#t3code

The package is maintained in nixpkgs and includes the desktop app () and the command. See Nix installation for NixOS configuration and updates.

We are very very early in this project. Expect bugs.

We are (mostly) not accepting contributions yet. Small fixes may be considered. Big features will not be.

Full docs live in docs/. There's no docs site yet.

If you REALLY want to contribute still.... read this first

T3 Code uses Vite+ so you'll need to install the global command-line tool.

curl -fsSL https://vite.plus | bash

irm https://vite.plus/ps1 | iex

items.title: mattpocock/skills
items.content:
Skills for Real Engineers. Straight from my .agents directory.

My agent skills that I use every day to do real engineering - not vibe coding.

Developing real applications is hard. Approaches like GSD, BMAD, and Spec-Kit try to help by owning the process. But while doing so, they take away your control and make bugs in the process hard to resolve.

These skills are designed to be small, easy to adapt, and composable. They work with any model. They're based on decades of engineering experience. Hack around with them. Make them your own. Enjoy.

If you want to keep up with changes to these skills, and any new ones I create, you can join ~60,000 other devs on my newsletter:

Installation (30-second setup)

A plugin updates itself. skills.sh copies editable files into your project, and you update them by hand. Pick one per agent, because installing both gives you every skill twice.

2. Run /setup-matt-pocock-skills

In your agent, run it once per repo. It will:

  • Ask you which issue tracker you want to use (GitHub, GitLab, local files, or anything else you describe)
  • Ask you what labels you apply to tickets when you triage them ( uses labels)
  • Ask you where you want to save any docs we create

3. Bam - you're ready to go.

I built these skills as a way to fix common failure modes I see with Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents.

#1: The Agent Didn't Do What I Want

. The most common failure mode in software development is misalignment. You think the dev knows what you want. Then you see what they've built - and you realize it didn't understand you at all.

This is just the same in the AI age. There is a communication gap between you and the agent. The fix for this is a - getting the agent to ask you detailed questions about what you're building.

These are my most popular skills. They help you align with the agent before you get started, and think deeply about the change you're making. Use them time you want to make a change.

#2: The Agent Is Way Too Verbose

With a ubiquitous language, conversations among developers and expressions of the code are all derived from the same domain model.

: At the start of a project, devs and the people they're building the software for (the domain experts) are usually speaking different languages.

I felt the same tension with my agents. Agents are usually dropped into a project and asked to figure out the jargon as they go. So they use 20 words where 1 will do.

for this is a shared language. It's a document that helps agents decode the jargon used in the project.

This is built into . It's a grilling session, but that helps you build a shared language with the AI, and document hard-to-explain decisions in ADR's.

It's hard to explain how powerful this is. It might be the single coolest technique in this repo. Try it, and see.

A shared language has many other benefits than reducing verbosity:

  • Variables, functions and files are named consistently, using the shared language
  • As a result, the codebase is easier to navigate for the agent
  • The agent also spends fewer tokens on thinking, because it has access to a more concise language

#3: The Code Doesn't Work

"Always take small, deliberate steps. The rate of feedback is your speed limit. Never take on a task that’s too big."

: Let's say that you and the agent are aligned on what to build. What happens when the agent produces crap?

It's time to look at your feedback loops. Without feedback on how the code it produces actually runs, the agent will be flying blind.

: You need the usual tranche of feedback loops: static types, browser access, and automated tests.

For automated tests, a red-green-refactor loop is critical. This is where the agent writes a failing test first, then fixes the test. This helps give the agent a consistent level of feedback that results in far better code.

I've built a you can slot into any project. It encourages red-green-refactor and gives the agent plenty of guidance on what makes good and bad tests.

For debugging, I've also built a skill that wraps best debugging practices into a disciplined loop, gated phase by phase.

#4: We Built A Ball Of Mud

: Most apps built with agents are complex and hard to change. Because agents can radically speed up coding, they also accelerate software entropy. Codebases get more complex at an unprecedented rate.

for this is a radical new approach to AI-powered development: caring about the design of the code.

This is built in to every layer of these skills:

  • quizzes you about which modules you're touching before creating a spec

And crucially, /improve-codebase-architecture surveys a codebase for deepening opportunities and hands you the candidates. I recommend running it on your codebase once every few days. It is a survey, not a rescue: on a genuinely old codebase it will find real candidates, but it won't untangle the mud for you.

Software engineering fundamentals matter more than ever. These skills are my best effort at condensing these fundamentals into repeatable practices, to help you ship the best apps of your career. Enjoy.

These split on one axis: who can invoke them. skills are reachable only when you type them (e.g. ); their job is to orchestrate. skills can be invoked by you reached for automatically by the agent when the task fits; they hold the reusable discipline. A user-invoked skill may invoke model-invoked skills, but never another user-invoked one.

Skills I use daily for code work.

  • : Ask which skill or flow fits your situation. A router over the user-invoked skills in this repo.
  • : Grilling session that also builds your project's domain model, sharpening terminology and updating and ADRs inline.
  • : Move issues through a state machine of triage roles.
  • : Scan a codebase for deepening opportunities, present them as a visual HTML report, then grill through whichever one you pick.
  • : Configure this repo for the engineering skills (issue tracker, triage labels, domain doc layout). Run once per repo before using the other engineering skills.
  • : Turn the current conversation into a spec and publish it to the issue tracker. No interview, just synthesizes what you've already discussed.
  • : Break any plan, spec, or conversation into a set of tracer-bullet tickets, each declaring its blocking edges, written as text in a local file, or as native blocking links on a real tracker.
  • : Build the work described by a spec or set of tickets, driving at pre-agreed seams and closing out with before committing.
  • : Implement a whole spec on one integration branch. Works the tickets as a task graph, running implementer subagents across the ready frontier for maximum concurrency, then closes out with .
  • : Plan a huge chunk of work, more than one agent session can hold, as a shared map of decision tickets on the issue tracker, and resolve them one at a time until the way to the destination is clear.
  • : Suggest improvements to the coding agent's environment (navigation, automated checks, coding standards, steering files, tooling) after a session, most severe first.
  • : Build a throwaway prototype to answer a design question, either a single shareable HTML file for state/logic questions, or several radically different UI variations toggleable from one route.
  • : Disciplined diagnosis loop for hard bugs and performance regressions: build a feedback loop that goes red on this bug → minimise → hypothesise → instrument → fix → regression-test.
  • : Investigate a question against high-trust primary sources and capture the findings as a cited Markdown file in the repo, run as a background agent.
  • : Test-driven development with a red-green-refactor loop. Builds features or fixes bugs one vertical slice at a time.
  • : Actively build and sharpen a project's domain model: challenge terms against the glossary, stress-test with edge-case scenarios, and update and ADRs inline.
  • : Shared discipline and vocabulary for designing deep modules: a lot of behaviour behind a small interface, placed at a clean seam, testable through that interface.
  • : Two-axis review of the diff since a fixed point: (does it follow the repo's coding standards, plus a Fowler smell baseline?) and (does it faithfully implement the originating issue/spec?), run as parallel sub-agents so neither pollutes the other.
  • : The shape a pull request body should take: a summary as the smallest visual that makes the change clear, before/after evidence that it works, and a merge-danger call (one-way or two-way door, plus blast radius).
  • : Generate an interactive bash wizard that walks a human through steps only they can perform: provisioning infrastructure, setting up credentials or CI secrets, walking an unfamiliar third-party dashboard, or running a one-off migration or cutover.

General workflow tools, not code-specific.

  • : Get relentlessly interviewed about a plan or design until every branch of the design tree is resolved.
  • : Compact the current conversation into a handoff document so another agent can continue the work.
  • : Teach the user a new skill or concept over multiple sessions, using the current directory as a stateful teaching workspace.
  • : Turn a decision you can't answer alone into a Markdown questionnaire for the one person who can, filled in async, or together over a meeting. It grills you about the send (who it's for, what you need back), not the subject.
  • : Fire this the moment a message doesn't land. The agent re-pitches it with the context you're missing, in plain English, using your vocabulary.
  • : Interview the user relentlessly about a plan, decision, or idea until every branch of the design tree is resolved. The reusable interview primitive behind , , , and improve-codebase-architecture.

items.title: Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios
items.content:
Turn Claude Code into a full game dev studio — 49 AI agents, 72 workflow skills, and a complete coordination system mirroring real studio hierarchy.

Turn a single Claude Code session into a full game development studio. 49 agents. 74 skills. One coordinated AI team.

Building a game solo with AI is powerful — but a single chat session has no structure. No one stops you from hardcoding magic numbers, skipping design docs, or writing spaghetti code. There's no QA pass, no design review, no one asking "does this actually fit the game's vision?"

solves this by giving your AI session the structure of a real studio. Instead of one general-purpose assistant, you get 49 specialized agents organized into a studio hierarchy — directors who guard the vision, department leads who own their domains, and specialists who do the hands-on work. Each agent has defined responsibilities, escalation paths, and quality gates.

The result: you still make every decision, but now you have a team that asks the right questions, catches mistakes early, and keeps your project organized from first brainstorm to launch.

Specialized subagents across design, programming, art, audio, narrative, QA, and production
Slash commands for every workflow phase (, , , , , , etc.)
Automated validation on commits, pushes, asset changes, design-doc reads, writes and registries, session lifecycle, agent audit trail, and gap detection
Path-scoped coding standards enforced when editing gameplay, engine, AI, UI, network code, scene and asset files, and more
Document templates for GDDs, UX specs, ADRs, sprint plans, HUD design, accessibility, and more

Agents are organized into three tiers, matching how real studios operate:

Tier 1 — Directors
  creative-director    technical-director    producer

Tier 2 — Department Leads
  game-designer        lead-programmer       art-director
  audio-director       narrative-director    qa-lead
  release-manager      localization-lead

Tier 3 — Specialists
  gameplay-programmer  engine-programmer     ai-programmer
  network-programmer   tools-programmer      ui-programmer
  systems-designer     level-designer        economy-designer
  technical-artist     sound-designer        writer
  world-builder        ux-designer           prototyper
  performance-analyst  devops-engineer       analytics-engineer
  security-engineer    qa-tester             accessibility-specialist
  live-ops-designer    community-manager

Each agent declares a model in its frontmatter: the three directors ask for Opus, and fifteen specialists name Sonnet, and the remaining thirty inherit your session's model. Treat the tiers as seniority of role, not as a billing plan — most of the studio runs on whatever model you are already using.

The template includes agent sets for all three major engines. Use the set that matches your project:

GDScript, Shaders, GDExtension
DOTS/ECS, Shaders/VFX, Addressables, UI Toolkit
GAS, Blueprints, Replication, UMG/CommonUI

Type in Claude Code to access all 74 skills:

(coordinate multiple agents on a single feature)

Does it produce games, or documents?

A fair question, and the answer is a measurement rather than a sample project. Four games were built from one brief at different levels and the documents each wrote before its first line of game code were counted:

Docs before first line of game code

All of them produced a running, tested game. Two blind reviewers and a human playtest then ranked the build — the extra 29 documents bought traceability, not a better game.

It runs the game and looks at it

The measurement above is about cost. The other half is whether the thing works, and for a game that means someone has to at it — a passing test says nothing about a menu drawn off-screen. So a story that changes anything the player sees is not closed until the game has been launched, observed, and a screenshot retained in . A parse check is not a run. This holds at every rigor level, including , where automated tests are waived but the look is not.

The games themselves are deliberately shipped here: this is a template you clone to start your own project, and somebody else's game in your repo is clutter, not evidence.

  • Claude Code — the native installer is recommended (npm install -g @anthropic-ai/claude-code also works, on Node.js 22+)
  • Python 3 — reads for every skill and hook; without it every setting silently falls back to its default
  • Bash — runs every hook; built into macOS and Linux, and on Windows it comes with Git for Windows
  • : jq (for hook validation)

Hooks fail gracefully if optional tools are missing — you just lose validation — with one deliberate exception: a commit that stages data JSON is blocked when there is no Python to validate it.

  1. :

    git clone https://github.com/Donchitos/Claude-Code-Game-Studios.git my-game
cd my-game

  2. Open Claude Code in the project's root folder (the one holding and ) and start a session:

    Starting it in a subfolder such as skips the project's hooks, deny rules and ask-first permission mode.

  3. — the system asks where you are (no idea, vague concept, clear design, existing work) and guides you to the right workflow. No assumptions.

    Or jump directly to a specific skill if you already know what you need:

    • — explore game ideas from scratch
    • — configure your engine if you already know
    • — analyze an existing project

at the repo root is the single source of truth for how the studio behaves on your project — engine, naming conventions, and a block that controls how much process every skill enforces. writes it for you; you rarely need to hand-edit it.

The one question that matters most is — , , or . It's a single front door over six separate knobs ( — which GDD sections are required, , , , — how many director agents review your work, and ), so asks it once instead of six times:

  • (default) — jam-game speed. No GDDs required, terse docs, minimal QA evidence, solo review. → → (a one-page brief) → → ↔ .
  • — 5 required GDD sections, balanced doc depth, standard QA evidence, lean review.
  • — all 8 GDD sections, thorough docs, full QA evidence on every story type, full director review.

is the default because the heavier tier costs more to reach working code without producing a better result, and gives nothing back when someone new picks the project up. Raise it in one call when your project grows — and will suggest it when they see the signs.

Two escape hatches keep one setting from being a blunt instrument. holds a single system to a higher standard than the rest of the project — your combat system gets the full treatment while everything else stays light. sets, per test type (logic, integration, visual, UI, config), whether missing evidence blocks a story or merely warns.

Any of the six underlying knobs can still be set individually if you want a mix (e.g. with — comprehensive but compact). Two of them — ( / / ) and — are also : rigor sets the team-wide default, but you can override them per-developer in a gitignored without touching the shared config. (how often the AI pauses to ask before it acts) sits outside rigor and is likewise personally overridable.

View or change any setting with the skill:

/settings                              # view effective config
/settings modes.review_mode            # view one setting
/settings modes.rigor=full             # write to project.yaml (team-wide)
/settings --local modes.review_mode=solo   # write to project.local.yaml (just you)

Full schema and per-setting behavior: .claude/docs/effects-map.md.

Already using an older version of this template? See UPGRADING.md for step-by-step migration instructions, a breakdown of what changed between versions, and which files are safe to overwrite vs. which need a manual merge.

CLAUDE.md                           # Master configuration
.claude/
  settings.json                     # Hooks, permissions, safety rules
  agents/                           # 49 agent definitions (markdown + YAML frontmatter)
  skills/                           # 74 slash commands (subdirectory per skill)
  hooks/                            # 18 scripts (bash) — 15 event hooks, two helpers they
                                    #   source (yaml-helper.sh, update-check.sh), and one
                                    #   opt-in diagnostic you wire yourself
  rules/                            # 14 path-scoped coding standards
  statusline.sh                     # Status line script (context%, model, stage, epic breadcrumb)
  docs/
    workflow-catalog.yaml           # 7-phase pipeline definition (read by /help)
    templates/                      # 62 document templates (+ per-section guidance)
src/                                # Game source code (Godot). The code root is
                                    #   ENGINE-SPECIFIC: Unity compiles only
                                    #   Assets/, Unreal builds from Source/<Module>/
assets/                             # Art, audio, VFX, shaders, data files
design/                             # GDDs, narrative docs, level designs
docs/                               # Technical documentation and ADRs
tests/                              # Test suites (unit, integration, performance, playtest)
tools/                              # Build and pipeline tools
prototypes/                         # Throwaway prototypes (isolated from src/)
production/                         # Sprint plans, milestones, release tracking
studio-tests/                       # QA for the skills and agents themselves — see below

Testing your customizations

CCGS is a template you are meant to edit. is how you check that an edited or newly written skill still holds up — a catalog of all 74 skills and 49 agents, per-category quality rubrics, behavioral specs, and templates for writing specs of your own.

/skill-test static [name]     # structural linter — 7 compliance checks
/skill-test category [name]   # category-specific quality rubric
/skill-test spec [name]       # behavioral spec assertions
/skill-test audit             # coverage report across skills and agents
/skill-improve [name]         # test-fix-retest loop; keeps or reverts on score change

It tests the , never your game — game tests live in .

Agents follow a structured delegation model:

  1. — directors delegate to leads, leads delegate to specialists
  2. — same-tier agents can consult each other but can't make binding cross-domain decisions
  3. — disagreements escalate up to the shared parent ( for design, for technical)
  4. — cross-department changes are coordinated by
  5. — agents don't modify files outside their domain without explicit delegation

Collaborative, Not Autonomous

This is an auto-pilot system. Every agent follows a strict collaboration protocol:

  1. — agents ask questions before proposing solutions
  2. — agents show 2-4 options with pros/cons
  3. — the user always makes the call
  4. — agents show work before finalizing
  5. — nothing gets written without your sign-off

You stay in control. The agents provide structure and expertise, not autonomy.

That is how a terminal session started at the project root behaves out of the box. The and automation settings, and Claude Code's own auto mode, trade some of these prompts for speed; see setup-requirements.md for the routes into auto mode.

run automatically on every session:

PreToolUse (Bash, PowerShell)Checks for hardcoded values, TODO format, JSON validity, design doc sections — exits early if the command is not
PreToolUse (Bash, PowerShell)Warns on pushes to protected branches, and on , , , and — exits early for any other command
Refuses a whole-file read of a design doc over 40 KB and answers with its headings, so the retry reads one section ()
Warns, never blocks, when a write would break a rule the skills state: a file they never overwrite, the config guard, the prototype boundary, a localization freeze
Warns when a write to the entity or TR-ID registry would delete or renumber an entry, or set a status its header does not list
Checks data-file JSON under , or , and asset naming in Godot's only — exits early if the file is under none of them
Shows current branch and recent commits for orientation
Detects fresh projects (suggests ) and missing design docs when code or prototypes exist
Logs the compaction (its output does not reach Claude — restores context afterwards)
Permission prompt, or idle about a minuteShows Windows toast notification via PowerShell
Every response end, in the backgroundArchives to session log and records git activity
Audit trail start — logs subagent invocation
Audit trail stop — completes subagent record
validate-agent-artifact.shWarns when a subagent stops without writing the file its brief named
Advises running after any change

: , , , , , and fire on every Bash, PowerShell, Read, Write or Edit tool call and exit immediately (exit 0) when the command or file path is not relevant. This is normal hook behavior — not a performance concern.

in auto-allow test runs and block dangerous operations (force push, , reading files) in both the Bash and PowerShell tools. Read-only commands such as , and need no rule: Claude Code runs them without asking. The rules match anywhere after , so a git command whose text only mentions followed later by or , followed by , or followed by — a commit message such as git commit -m "push + pull" included — is denied too: reword the message.

Coding standards are automatically enforced based on file location. The paths below are Godot's. Each rule also matches the Unity and Unreal layouts: the code rules match C# under and C++ under (and , , , ), data matches JSON under and , shaders match by file type, and tests match C# under and C++ under .

Data-driven values, delta time usage, no UI references
Zero allocations in hot paths, thread safety, API stability
Performance budgets, debuggability, data-driven parameters
Server-authoritative, versioned messages, security
No game state ownership, localization-ready, accessibility
Required sections per , formula format, edge cases
Lore consistency, character voice, canon levels
JSON validity, naming conventions, schema rules
Naming conventions, performance targets, cross-platform rules
Scene and resource files changed in the editor where possible; safe hand-edit rules
Test naming, coverage requirements, fixture patterns
Relaxed standards, README required, hypothesis documented

This template is grounded in professional game development practices:

  • — Mechanics, Dynamics, Aesthetics analysis for game design
  • Self-Determination Theory — Autonomy, Competence, Relatedness for player motivation
  • — Challenge-skill balance for player engagement
  • — Audience targeting and validation
  • Verification-Driven Development — Tests first, then implementation

This is a , not a locked framework. Everything is meant to be customized:

  • — delete agent files you don't need, add new ones for your domains
  • — tune agent behavior, add project-specific knowledge
  • — adjust workflows to match your team's process
  • — create new path-scoped rules for your project's directory structure
  • — adjust validation strictness, add new checks
  • — use the Godot, Unity, or Unreal agent set (or none)
  • — and its underlying knobs in (see Configuration). Override per-run with on any skill.

Primary development on with Git Bash. The hooks and scripts are also tested on — its stock bash 3.2 and BSD tools, with and without — and on . All hooks use POSIX-compatible patterns (, not ) and include fallbacks for missing tools. The hook uses PowerShell for Windows toast notifications and is a no-op elsewhere — desktop notifications on macOS/Linux are not yet wired. Please file issues for any platform-specific breakage.

Claude Code Game Studios is free and open source. If it saves you time or helps you ship your game, consider supporting continued development:

Sponsorships help fund time spent maintaining skills, adding new agents, keeping up with Claude Code and engine API changes, and responding to community issues.
