items.title: Panniantong/Agent-Reach
items.content:
Give your AI agent eyes to see the entire internet. Read & search Twitter, Reddit, YouTube, GitHub, Bilibili, XiaoHongShu — one CLI, zero API fees.

登录墙后的平台、视频里的内容、中文平台、干净的结构化数据，一条命令拿到

Agent Reach 让你的 Agent 真正连上互联网，用上它自己够不着的平台和能力。

Claude Code、Codex、Hermes Agent、OpenClaw 这类 CLI Agent 自带搜索和网页读取，但下面这些它们基本够不着：

  • ：在小红书搜笔记、在 X 查账号动态、读职位详情等。
  • ：B站和 YouTube 的字幕，以及 YouTube 视频、小宇宙播客的语音转文字。
  • ：B站、小红书、V2EX、雪球，通用搜索覆盖很差。
  • ：雪球行情、V2EX 帖子和回复、GitHub 仓库和 issue，拿到的是整理好的内容。

Agent Reach 把这些平台背后的工具替你装好、测好，Agent 一条命令就能用：

agent-reach channels                          # 有哪些渠道、每个渠道能做什么
agent-reach bilibili search "大模型"           # agent-reach <渠道> <动作> [参数]
agent-reach read https://www.v2ex.com/t/123   # 按链接自动选渠道
  • 一切 Agent 都能用。
  • 要登录的平台用 Agent Reach 自己的专用浏览器，在后台运行、不弹窗。第一次用某个网站时，会把你 Chrome 里这个网站的登录复制一份过去，原浏览器不变，不读密码库。复制过来的通常是主账号，建议换成小号，做法见下面的"安全性"。详见会话配置。
搜仓库、读仓库/README、读 issue 和 PR（含评论）
无；转文字需要 Groq 或 OpenAI Key
  • ：装好就能用；不想要也可以去掉，以后更新不会再加回来。
  • ：说一句"帮我加上 XX"就开启，需要的软件会自动装好。
帮我安装 Agent Reach：https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Panniantong/Agent-Reach/main/docs/install.md

剩下的 Agent 自己做完。过程中你可能会被问到：

  • ：如果 Agent 说自己不能运行命令，去它的设置里打开"允许执行命令"。
  • ：uv 是一个安装命令行程序的小工具，不需要管理员密码。电脑上没有的话 Agent 会先装它，会跟你说一声。
  • ：装完后 Agent 会告诉你哪些已经能用（B站、V2EX、GitHub、YouTube、网页），以及还能加哪些。你选了再加，也可以以后随时说"帮我加上小红书"，一条命令就装好。

关于登录：部分平台会直接复用你电脑上已有的登录。想换成某个特定账号（比如小号），跟 Agent 说一声就行。Agent 从不替你登录，也不会要你的密码。

⚠️ PyPI 上叫 的包不是本项目，请勿从 PyPI 安装，只用 install.md 里的 GitHub 地址。

Agent Reach 装的所有东西（各渠道的工具、登录、设置）都放在你电脑上同一个文件夹里（），不散落到别处。所以升级、管理、删除都很省事，一句话就行。

告诉你每个渠道现在能不能用，哪些是上次还好、现在坏了
开启并装好它需要的一切 / 关掉它，清掉它的登录和专用工具
"小红书登录过期了" / "换个账号" / "退出登录"打开登录窗口，由你本人登录 / 清掉这个网站的登录

每个平台的每个动作都有一个按顺序尝试的工具列表。比如读 B站视频先用 bili-cli，失败了自动换 B站公开接口；读网页先用 Jina Reader，再用 Exa。

flowchart LR
    A[Agent] -->|agent-reach 渠道 动作| B[Agent Reach]
    B --> C{按顺序尝试}
    C -->|首选| D[上游工具 1]
    C -->|失败时备选| E[上游工具 2]
    D --> F[结果]
    E --> F
    F --> A

平台改版、工具失效是常态。换工具只是调整这个列表，Agent 的用法不变。

  • ：只搜索和读取，不发帖、不评论、不点赞、不私信。
  • 部分平台会复用你电脑上已有的登录（只复制这一个网站，原浏览器不变）；确实需要重新登录时才打开专用窗口，由你本人完成。
  • 复用过来的通常是主账号，而平台可能限制自动访问的账号。想换成小号，跟 Agent 说一声就行。
  • ：在你自己的终端里运行 agent-reach configure groq-key 填写。

跟 Agent 说"卸载 Agent Reach"。它会先列出要删的东西，你确认后再删。只删 Agent Reach 自己装的东西，你的其他文件和浏览器都不动。最后它会告诉你怎么删掉程序本身。

    有相关合作，或者想加交流群，加我微信，或直接加入 Discord 社区：

    Agent Reach 没有官方代币、币、投资产品、领取手续费活动、钱包连接，也没有 Solana/Pump.fun 项目。任何借用 Agent Reach 名字、GitHub 地址或作者身份的加密项目都与本仓库无关，请勿据此连接钱包或领取任何费用。

    Agent Skills Hub — 找 Claude 技能和 MCP 服务器，不用猜哪个安全：133,000+ 个条目全部安全分级、质量评分，每 8 小时刷新。

items.title: nightly-labs/openbot
items.content:
A local-first desktop workspace for persistent AI teammates. Run Codex, Claude, and Grok with dedicated workspaces, task queues, file sharing, browser control, and agent-to-agent collaboration.

OpenBot is a local-first desktop workspace for persistent AI teammates. It supports the local Codex App Server and Claude Code, plus Grok CLI, OpenCode, Gemini, Cursor CLI, and Cline CLI through ACP. It gives every agent its own workspace and conversation, and provides local queues, file transfers, an embedded browser, and agent-to-agent messaging in one desktop app.

OpenBot is a development preview. Agents currently run with and . They can read and modify files, run commands, use the network, and control the embedded browser without per-action confirmations after the explicit first-launch consent. Run only agents and tasks you trust, keep backups, and review Security before use.

  • Prompt-driven agent creation and editing on desktop and mobile, with editable instructions, avatar, and section review before saving.
  • Persistent agents backed by independent Codex, Claude, Grok, OpenCode, Gemini, Cursor, or Cline sessions and local workspaces.
  • Custom OpenAI-compatible endpoints and custom ACP agents, with detection of local model servers (Ollama, LM Studio) and installed agents.
  • Per-agent context monitoring with automatic compaction before long threads exhaust the model window.
  • FIFO message queues with pause, resume, cancellation, and crash-safe persistence.
  • Agent-to-agent messages, replies, reactions, images, and managed file transfers.
  • Shared desktop channel chats with one task owner, explicit delegation, shared history, and Stop, Resume, Reassign, Archive, and Restore controls.
  • A persistent embedded browser that agents can open, inspect, and control.
  • Optional Computer Use on macOS, Windows and Linux through the binary in the release, which OpenBot starts as its own child process and gives to every provider.
  • Per-agent model, reasoning, profile, notification, browser, and panel state.
  • Local data and privacy-safe diagnostics exports from the account menu.
  • Optional OpenBot accounts through one-time email codes. The account API runs on Cloudflare Workers and D1.

OpenBot is local-first, not offline-only. Codex connects to OpenAI, Claude connects to Anthropic, Grok connects to xAI, Gemini connects to Google, Cursor connects to Cursor, Cline connects to Cline, visited pages use the network, and installed plugins may connect to their own services.

OpenBot supports macOS 13 or newer on Apple silicon or Intel, Windows 10 or newer on x64 systems, and x64 or arm64 Linux as an AppImage.

  1. Download the latest (or on an Intel Mac) from GitHub Releases.
  2. Drag OpenBot to Applications and open it.
  1. Run the installer and open OpenBot.
  1. Download the latest OpenBot-*-x86_64.AppImage (or on arm64) from GitHub Releases.
  2. Make it executable with chmod +x OpenBot-*.AppImage, then run it.

The AppImage does not need libfuse2, so it also runs on Arch Linux and Omarchy. It mounts itself with from the package.

On Ubuntu 23.10 or newer and on Debian 13, unprivileged user namespaces are restricted by AppArmor and OpenBot exits during launch until you install an AppArmor profile:

sudo install -m 0644 build/linux/openbot.apparmor /etc/apparmor.d/openbot
sudo systemctl reload apparmor

The same file ships inside the AppImage at resources/linux/openbot.apparmor. Edit the attachment path in the profile if you keep the AppImage outside the usual locations. Do not start OpenBot with : that removes the boundary between a renderer and the rest of the computer.

On the first start from an AppImage, OpenBot writes ~/.local/share/applications/openbot.desktop and ~/.local/share/icons/openbot.png, which is what lets an link - an invitation, or a plugin listing - open the app and gives the launcher an icon that stays after the app exits. Delete the two files to undo it.

Remote desktop works on Linux x64 in an X11 session, such as Xorg or Xvfb. It does not work under Wayland, and the arm64 AppImage does not include it.

For Gemini sign-in, install a desktop browser and . Open the sign-in page in a desktop session on the same host or VM. Google sends the callback to that host through ; a server with no desktop cannot complete this sign-in. See Gemini setup.

Linux server with no screen

To run OpenBot as an always-on server of your account on a VPS or home server (Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04 with systemd), install it from a terminal and sign in with an email code:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nightly-labs/openbot/main/scripts/install-server.sh | sudo bash
sudo openbot login

Then use it from the desktop app, the iPhone app or . See self-hosted servers for the options and the commands.

The same server runs as a container ( and ). The seccomp profile lets the Electron sandbox stay on:

curl -fsSLO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/nightly-labs/openbot/main/docker/seccomp.json
docker run -d --name openbot --restart unless-stopped \
  --security-opt seccomp=seccomp.json --security-opt no-new-privileges:true \
  --shm-size 1g --stop-timeout 60 -v openbot-data:/data \
  ghcr.io/nightly-labs/openbot:latest
docker exec -it openbot openbot login

See Docker for Compose, the data volume, upgrades and the security limits. For Amazon ECS, see AWS ECS.

The flake installs the desktop app from the latest release on x64 or arm64 Linux and on Apple silicon:

nix run github:nightly-labs/openbot
nix profile install github:nightly-labs/openbot

adds . OpenBot is not free software, so your nixpkgs must allow it, for example with nixpkgs.config.allowUnfreePredicate = pkg: lib.getName pkg == "openbot";. Nix installs OpenBot updates. OpenBot does not update itself from the Nix store. On Linux, the Nix package does not include the remote desktop runtime, because nixpkgs does not have a library that it needs.

Windows releases are signed by SYNTHETIFY LABS SPÓŁKA Z OGRANICZONĄ ODPOWIEDZIALNOŚCIĄ. Older releases are not code-signed. SmartScreen can still warn about a new release. Check the release checksum or GitHub build attestation before you run the installer.

OpenBot can download a supported provider runtime when you select in onboarding, Settings, agent setup, or the model picker. OpenBot prefers its managed CLI. Explicit overrides take precedence; a compatible system CLI is used when no managed copy is available. OpenBot checks for a newer provider CLI release at startup and every hour, and in a provider's actions menu checks at once. Updates install the latest upstream release without changing the user’s system CLI; the version in is only the first-install fallback.

You can also install a CLI yourself.

curl -fsSL https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.sh | sh

curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash

Install Grok CLI following the Grok Build documentation, then authenticate with or set in the environment used to launch OpenBot.

OpenBot downloads and pins the OpenCode CLI, like Codex, Claude, and Grok. OpenCode's free models need no account and no sign-in: select OpenCode, click Connect, and OpenBot reads the models that the CLI advertises. To use the paid OpenCode Go models, click Sign in on the OpenCode row and paste a Go key from opencode.ai/auth. OpenBot encrypts the key on this computer and gives it only to the local CLI. OpenBot supports OpenCode Go only: the Zen models a Go key does not buy stay out of the picker. Models with the Free label in the model picker need no sign-in. Other models need a sign-in with their provider: a Go key for the models, or in a terminal for OpenCode Zen and third-party providers. Without it, the turn fails with an error that names the provider. If you installed OpenCode yourself, OpenBot keeps that install and offers no download. Set to select an executable outside your shell's search path. Remote OpenCode agents require Team API v4; older clients do not show these agents.

Gemini uses a Google AI Pro or Ultra plan. OpenBot downloads Google's Antigravity ACP server on this computer when you select Download on the Gemini row, because Google's license does not let OpenBot include it. Sign in opens Google's sign-in page in your browser. OpenBot never uses an command on your search path, because the Antigravity editor installs a command with that name. Set to select a server executable yourself. Put it in a folder, and put an file with its in the folder above . Keep beside the server. When that path is set, OpenBot uses only it. Connect remains available in the host's local Settings > Providers screen. Remote settings cannot perform Google sign-in; use a browser on the host. See Gemini setup and download recovery for the required layout, the reported IPv6 download failure, and checks that do not change host networking.

Cursor uses a Cursor plan or a Cursor API key. OpenBot downloads and pins the Cursor CLI () when you select Download on the Cursor row in More providers, and starts it with . Sign in opens Cursor's sign-in page in your browser. You can also set in the environment used to launch OpenBot. If you installed yourself, OpenBot uses it until a download exists. OpenBot never uses the command, which starts the Cursor editor. Set to select an executable yourself. Cursor agents stay on this computer: team members do not see them.

Cline uses a Cline account, which has free models with limits for each model. The provider of a free model can use your prompts to train models. OpenBot downloads and pins the Cline CLI () when you select Download on the Cline row in More providers, and starts it with . Sign in opens Cline's sign-in page in your browser. You can also set in the environment used to launch OpenBot. If you installed 3.0.68 or newer yourself, OpenBot uses it until a download exists. Set to select an executable yourself. Cline agents stay on this computer: team members do not see them.

On Windows, install the native CLI and make sure , , or is available in PowerShell. Claude Code also requires Git for Windows. Then authenticate the installed CLI and restart OpenBot.

Bun and Node.js are not required when using an installed release. Optional Computer Use works on macOS, Windows and Linux, and the release carries the driver, so there is nothing to install. Only macOS asks for a permission for it: Screen Recording and Accessibility.

OpenBot uses the existing local CLI login. It does not copy provider credentials. Grok's and per-session MCP bearer tokens are never persisted or logged. Each provider's terms apply to your sign-in. See provider terms for Claude subscriptions.

For setup problems, data reset, and uninstall instructions, see Troubleshooting. OpenBot's data and network behavior is documented in Privacy.

Development requires stable Bun 1.4.2, Node.js 24 (the version in , matching the Node that Electron bundles - run ), and at least one supported agent CLI.

Install the exact Bun version on macOS or Linux:

curl -fsSL https://bun.com/install | bash -s "bun-v1.4.2"

Install it on Windows in PowerShell:

iex "& {$(irm https://bun.com/install.ps1)} -Version 1.4.2"

git clone https://github.com/nightly-labs/openbot.git
cd openbot
bun install --frozen-lockfile
bun run codex:doctor
bun run dev

checks the CLI version, App Server handshake, and ChatGPT login without starting a model turn. bun run cua-driver:doctor reports the Computer Use driver separately.

In a new git worktree, run . It copies the files that lists from the main checkout when they are missing, installs dependencies, migrates the local API, and seeds the isolated profile. Set it as the worktree setup command of your agent harness.

On macOS, a worktree's uses almost no new disk space. Bun clones packages from its cache, and the root clones Electron from ~/Library/Caches/OpenBot/electron-dist. still shows the full size of each clone. The first install of an Electron version extracts it once and saves it there. Delete the directory to clear the cache; an entry that nobody used for 30 days is removed by the next save.

To reset only the local development state, quit the dev app and test client, then run . The command deletes the app and test-client development profiles plus the legacy host profile, including and its WAL files. It prints each profile before it deletes it, and it deletes nothing while a dev app has one of them open. It does not change the production profile, the worktree profiles that opens (), agent workspaces, , or .

seeds a development profile it creates, so a first start already shows this data. replaces the shared profile. To use it, quit the dev app, then run:

bun run dev:seed
bun run dev --shared

The seeded agents run on opencode-go/muse-spark-1.3-contributor at medium effort while this computer's OpenCode CLI lists it, and on at low effort otherwise. A dev build starts a new agent on the same pair, so a seeded agent and one you create agree; a packaged build always uses .

The seed adds agents, rich conversations, managed files and references, reactions, completed agent exchanges, two channels with a delegated task run, channel memories and routines, and local team chat data. It dates every record backwards from the run, so the transcripts read Today and Yesterday. It does not add live queue items, open routine runs, or queued channel tasks, so it starts no model turn. Use bun run dev:seed --dry-run to inspect the target and fixture counts without changing files. , , , , and print their usage for and change nothing. They stop with exit code 2 on an option that they do not know.

Marketplace launch catalog

Seed the approved OpenBot team catalog locally with bun run marketplace:seed:local, then start or reuse . Search in Marketplace to review its Skills and Agents. This seed adds catalog records without resetting app data.

bun run marketplace:build creates the launch bundles. bun run marketplace:publish:production is a dry run; production writes require explicit flags and admin credentials. See the catalog and publication guide.

Skill authors can add optional text to the YAML frontmatter in :

example-prompt: Turn the latest commits into release notes.

The skill preview shows this text. appends it and a skill reference to the selected agent's draft. It does not send the message. The field accepts up to 1,000 characters after trimming. Missing or invalid values use a default example. No new package format or database migration is required.

Ask an agent to create a skill from a reusable workflow. It prepares a folder with and calls . The skill is saved in a shared local library and enabled for that agent. Other agents can add it through Settings → Skills → Local skills.

Agents can use , , , and . Revisions require the version read by the agent and retain previous versions. Updating a library skill does not update installed copies: use the Update chip or install an exact revision. Modified installed files are protected. To publish a local skill, submit its folder separately through the marketplace.

Optional scripts, references, and assets follow the Codex skill folder structure. A PNG at supplies the local preview logo. The built-in guide explains the format and validation limits. Registration does not run scripts.

Import agents from Grok Bot

Open on this computer, or on a joined server in the desktop app or the browser client. Every member of a server can import, not only an owner or admin. Add the OpenBot export agent to Grok Bot and say "Export my agents for OpenBot". It saves one file to Downloads. Choose that file in OpenBot, select the agents, and import them.

The import adds each agent's name, instructions, avatar, skills, routines, and memories. Workspace files are copied to in the agent's workspace if you included them. Chat history is not copied: the export agent keeps the important facts as memories. For this computer, the file is read here and is not uploaded. For a joined server, the file (at most 100 MB) goes to the computer that runs that server through the encrypted host connection. A member's import uses a skill that the server already has instead of changing it. The export skill and its format are in resources/agent-import/grok-bot/SKILL.md.

The browser client is served at by the public web app. For local development, run and open on the API URL printed by the supervisor. Use when a desktop host is also needed. Use and Web → Workspace → Connected for shared UI test data. See web client delivery for the release gate and focused checks.

Start the local Auth API, Signal service, and Electron client with renderer HMR on its app profile. Ports are allocated through the dev registry, so a sibling worktree never takes one this stack won. It refuses a second stack in the same worktree unless you pass . Each worktree opens a profile of its own, keyed to its path; opens the shared profile instead. is still accepted and changes nothing. A profile that you used before stays on disk unchanged. signs the app in to the account Worker, on a profile that all worktrees share, so that a hosted server is a real VM; see docs/hosted-servers.md. A profile that does not exist yet is seeded with the showcase data of before the client starts, so a first start never opens an empty app; an existing profile is left as it is. An isolated profile still shares the computer's provider CLI store, so it does not download the pinned CLIs again. Before it starts, it runs bun install --frozen-lockfile and bun run api:migrate:local only when , a workspace , a patch, or a migration changed since their last successful run. The stamps are in and apps/auth-api/.wrangler/state/v3/d1, and each writes the install stamp too; delete one to run its step again.
Preview the built Electron client with the green preview icon.
Start the mobile app in Expo Go and clear the Metro cache.
Build and launch the iOS simulator app without RocketSim.
Start or reuse this worktree's stack, build and launch the iOS simulator app, and pair them without a QR scan. The desktop issues a Mobile Connect ticket over CDP, and opens the link in the development build, which accepts only loopback or private-network account services. Other arguments go to . pairs an app that already runs; chooses one of several booted simulators. It stops when the Metro port is already in use, because another worktree's Metro would serve the same app id; pass then.
bun run mobile:ios:build:localBuild a production iOS locally for upload with Transporter. See TestFlight setup.
bun run mobile:ios:release:testflightStart the GitHub Actions iOS build from and upload to TestFlight. Requires authenticated GitHub CLI. See iOS release setup.
Start RocketSim and build and launch the iOS simulator app with RocketSim Connect. See mobile setup.
Start the mobile app in Expo Go through a Metro tunnel and clear the cache. The OpenBot API and Signal still need their own reachable addresses.
Start the TanStack Start API and its local D1 database on .
bun run dev:apns-key -- <AuthKey_ID.p8> [KEY_ID]Save an Apple Push Notification service key in ignored development state, so the local Auth API sends iPhone Live Activity updates. The local server forwards them to Apple over HTTP/2. Restart after it.
Build and preview the Cloudflare Worker locally.
Draw the article artwork into apps/auth-api/content-art/ after you add an article or change a title. Commit the result; the site build fails until it matches. Needs Electron and a GPU, so run it on your own machine.
bun run api:migrate:localApply D1 migrations to the local development database.
bun run api:migrate:remoteApply D1 migrations to the configured remote database.
Build and deploy the account API to Cloudflare Workers. It sets the Stripe, boat, claim and OpenPanel secret sets that are in the production environment. A set that is not there keeps the value that the Worker has.
bun run api:stripe:bootstrapCreate or update the Stripe plan catalog and the Customer Portal settings from in the encrypted (shell values replace it). It refuses a live key unless you add . For local webhooks, run stripe listen --forward-to localhost:<API port>/v1/stripe/webhook and set the signing secret in . See Billing.
bun run hosting:setup --target=production|testSet up the Stripe catalog, the Customer Portal, and the Stripe and boat webhooks of one account server, and store the webhook signing secrets: production in the GitHub Environment, test in the encrypted . See hosted servers.
Build the boat named snapshot that new hosted servers start from. Needs and , , and . See hosted servers.
Build the public status page in . The workflow adds and and publishes it to GitHub Pages at .
Run the status page smoke test: update runs against a local fake service, the status webhooks against a local receiver, one read-only run against the live checks, and the built page in Chrome. It writes .openbot-build/status-page/report.json.
Build and start the self-hosted Signal, coturn, and ACME stack.
Check the Remote API and both Docker Compose configurations.
bun run remote:check:composeValidate both Docker Compose configurations alone, without a running daemon.
Update Signal, then drain and update the single coturn instance.
Start the Auth API, Signal service, and single local Electron instance.
Start the same stack as , with two quick tunnels, one to Signal and one to the local account API, so that Slack can send the development Slack app's events and install return to the agents on this computer. It reads OPENBOT_DEV_SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET from the ignored , and needs and in the shell environment. Takes the same options as , such as . See docs/messaging.md.
Start the Auth API, Signal service, local instance, and an isolated second client for team testing.
Replace only the app development profile with durable showcase data. keeps an existing profile, which is how seeds a first start. --scale=agents:N,messages:M,channels:C,channelMessages:K,attachments:A adds generated agents, chat history, channel history and large images to the showcase data, for memory and CPU measurements.
Delete the local app, test-client, and legacy host development state. It refuses while a dev app has one of these profiles open.
Print, as JSON, every dev stack and dev app instance live on this machine: services, ports, pids, which of them belong to this worktree, and which are orphaned - a supervisor that is gone with its children still holding the ports. Each recorded process carries the state a stop command acts on: , with for a survivor of a dead leader, and for a pid this machine cannot date. is the directory it read: ~/Library/Caches/OpenBot/dev on macOS, $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/openbot-dev (else ) on Linux, %LOCALAPPDATA%\OpenBot\openbot-dev-instances on Windows, or when set. It does not depend on .
Print a stable JSON verification plan for this worktree: / for safe checks, setup state, changed files and affected surfaces, nearby tests, runtime state, //, the renderer QA loop, safe , and all suggested . Add to execute only the safe non-mutating checks in the plan. Renderer QA follows snapshot → action with --wait-for → snapshot → screenshot when appearance matters.
Stop this worktree's dev stack, children included, using the pids in the registry rather than a process-name pattern. It signals only a pid whose start time still matches the record, so a recycled pid is never sent SIGTERM; anything it cannot confirm is reported, left running and kept in the registry, and the command exits non-zero. stops one other stack, stops every stack on the machine.
Drop this worktree's stack record without signalling anything, for the one case refuses to resolve on its own. It is also the only command that reads a dead record: nothing else deletes one, because a reader that removes what it judged can remove a record the supervisor rewrote in between. Takes the same and .
Start Storybook on a port allocated through the same registry, so two worktrees never announce one port. moves where the search starts; is refused.
Build static Storybook. CI sets OPENBOT_STORYBOOK_CHECK=true to skip automatic prop documentation during its build check.
Drive the running dev app over CDP: , , , , / by accessible role. --page=<target-id|url-substring> aims at any window, including embedded browser views; settles on an accessible target instead of polling; mutations need and a named instance (this worktree's record, or ).
Measure idle CPU on the running dev app, per process kind and per page. (default 60000), (default 5000), , (always under .openbot-build/dev-automation/cpu/, and refused if it would leave that directory or pass through a symbolic link) and for a before/after delta. Read-only. Take a baseline before a change and a second run after it: only the difference between two runs on the same machine is a result, because a dev build carries the Vite server and the source maps as well.
Measure the running dev app's memory once: resident memory per process kind (main, renderer, GPU, provider CLIs and their MCP servers), with the dev tooling kept out of the app total, plus JS heap and DOM counters per page. , (always under .openbot-build/dev-automation/memory/) and --heap-snapshot=<target-id|url-substring> to also write a V8 heap snapshot of one page to that directory. Read-only.
Run repeatable RAM and CPU scenarios on the built app ( first). Each run seeds a bench profile of its own, starts the built app, samples the process tree every second (resident memory, macOS physical footprint and CPU per process kind, provider memory per CLI) with the main-process and page heaps, drives the scenario, and reads a settled state after garbage collection. --scenario=<id|prefix|all> (required; without it the command lists the scenarios), (default 3; the report shows the median and range), , , (records the app window's JavaScript for 15 s after the first run settles, as a for DevTools), (counts frames slower than 17 ms and 50 ms while the scenario runs; the loop keeps the renderer drawing, so CPU readings rise) and (V8 call counts per function while the scenario runs, top 25 in a file; slows JavaScript). Every run also reports the startup marks (, ms) and the app window's layout and style recalculation counts, script and task time, and long tasks (). Reports go to .openbot-build/dev-automation/bench/. Turn scenarios ( to ) use the real claude, opencode and grok CLIs and spend model quota. It never touches a dev instance or your own profile, and stops an app a failed run left behind.
Run Biome, both typechecks, offline tests, the browser smoke test, and the production build.
Check all 15 projects in parallel with a separate incremental cache for each project in this worktree.
Find unused files, exports, and types, unused or unlisted dependencies, and unresolved imports in all workspaces. CI runs it.
Check the renderer against the design system: shared primitives, Kobalte and Lucide confined to , palette tokens instead of colour, size, radius and transition literals. Checks renderer and shared UI source.
Fail when a tracked image or video file is outside the product asset directories. Pull request screenshots go in the pull request body.
Fail when a link in a tracked Markdown file names a Markdown file that does not exist, or an anchor that the file does not have.
After , run the built preload with a fake Electron. Fail when it loads a module that a sandboxed preload cannot load, uses , or exposes a method that does not name.
Hold each TypeScript option in tools/typescript/type-baseline.json to its error count per file in every project that extends . A new error fails. Add after a fix to lower the baseline, or to start an option at its current counts.
Check the translation catalogs: key prefixes, placeholders, plural forms, ambiguous source text, and unused keys. puts translated keys in the English order. writes .openbot-build/i18n-report.json. See docs/i18n.md.
Run, on one worker, only the desktop and mobile test files that import a file changed since , including staged, unstaged and untracked files. It stops with an error when is missing. A change to a vitest config, a setup file or selects no test. See docs/development-checks.md.
bun run test:related -- <source>...Run, on one worker, only the test files that import the named source files.
bun run test:browser-agent-sessionCheck that an agent with its own browser session, and the agents of a named browser profile, keep their cookies and storage apart, across popups, a restart, a deleted profile, and a clear.
bun run test:browser-profile-agentsCheck that the shared profile, an agent's own session, a named profile, and the delete of a named profile change the stored browser profile of an agent, and that the choice stays after a restart.
Run the complete local embedded-browser smoke test, including cross-process persistence. Use , , , --scenario=wait-deadlines, or for one isolated scenario.
Probe the real CLI handshake and account without starting a paid turn.
Re-record how long each desktop test file takes. CI splits its shards by this table, so run it when the two shards stop finishing together.
bun run cua-driver:doctorPrint, as JSON, which binary OpenBot would use for Computer Use, and the driver's own report. Read-only, and it starts no daemon. selects a different binary in a checkout; an installed application runs only the driver it was released with.
bun run prepare:cua-driverWrite the pinned Computer Use driver to build/cua-driver/<platform>/<arch>, verifying every SHA-256 in . Name another target with bun scripts/install-cua-driver.ts <platform> <arch>. Every packaging command runs this first.
bun run pin:cua-driver <version>Print a new block for from a published release. Downloads the release assets of all five targets and hashes each shipped file.
Build an unpacked local application for the architecture of this Mac.
Build and verify the real app bundle for this Mac, icon, metadata, ASAR, and fuses.
Build an unpacked local Windows x64 application on Windows.
bun run package:win:verifyBuild and verify the Windows x64 application on Windows.
Build an unpacked local Linux x64 application on Linux.
bun run package:linux:arm64Build an unpacked local Linux arm64 application on arm64 Linux.
bun run package:linux:verifyBuild and verify the Linux x64 application on Linux. Run it under without a display.
bun scripts/create-github-app.ts [--org <org>]Create the OpenBot GitHub App from scripts/github-app/manifest.json with the manifest flow. Prints the Client ID for src/main/github-connector-config.ts and writes the app secrets to ~/.config/openbot/github-app-<slug>.json (mode 0600). Enable Device Flow in the app settings after the run.
bun run release:preflightVerify version, Git state, and GitHub release secrets before tagging.
Build unsigned local DMG and ZIP update artifacts for this Mac.
Build an unsigned Windows x64 NSIS installer on Windows.
Build an unsigned Linux x64 AppImage on Linux.
Build an unsigned Linux arm64 AppImage on arm64 Linux.
Create the next patch version commit and tag.
bun run mobile:release:patchMove the iPhone app notes from into and set the next patch version in . Also and .
bun run mobile:release:published <ios|android|both>Write today's date for a store that made the mobile build available. shows each store, and a store that still reviews the build as "In review". Add for a version that is not in .
bun run test:acp-directoriesRun three fake ACP agents through the provider driver: new, load and resume requests carry the workspace roots as only when the agent advertises them. Offline; writes .openbot-build/acp-additional-directories-e2e/report.json.
bun run test:custom-agentsRun two fake ACP agents through the agent store, Check agent (with its model list) and the provider router: equal session ids, restart and resume, switch, and delete. Offline; writes .openbot-build/custom-acp-agent-e2e/report.json.
bun run test:mcp-tool-consentRun the real Codex app-server with a fake model, a real MCP server and the real attention registry: tool consent at Ask first and Full access, Always allow and a restart, refusals, and the requests that stay with the user (forms, sign-in, look-alikes). Needs a Codex CLI; offline; writes .openbot-build/mcp-tool-consent-e2e/report.json.
Run the real attention registry and Team API codecs on blocks: answers from the owner, an admin, a member and a released client, the member refusal for privileged actions, a secret form value that is never stored, skip and expiry, and the wire on protocols 6 and 7. Offline; writes .openbot-build/ui-blocks-e2e/report.json.
run real full-access Codex and Claude filesystem turns across private and shared workspaces.
run a real full-access image-generation turn.
bun run test:workspace-only run real Workspace only Codex, Claude, Grok and OpenCode turns that try to write outside; writes a JSON report per provider to .openbot-build/workspace-only-smoke/. Add for one, and to choose its model.
bun run test:provider-detectionRun local detection, Load models and endpoint Edit against fake OpenAI-compatible servers on this computer: no key in a scan, no redirect, the stored key only to its own origin. Offline; writes .openbot-build/provider-detection-e2e/report.json.
bun run test:storage-live verify isolated Codex and Claude turns in a temporary SQLite database.

Publishing never creates a second OpenBot instance. The host keeps its Team API on loopback. A hidden, sandboxed Electron page connects it to invited clients through WebRTC. Signal carries only connection setup messages. Team data uses direct DataChannels when possible and the project coturn service when direct ICE fails. Cloudflare stores accounts, configuration, memberships, invitations, logical session records, and public assets. It does not carry chats, files, commands, or remote desktop media.

The development runner advertises both Mobile Connect and its Signal service on the preferred private LAN interface. Restart the runner after changing networks so newly generated QR codes contain the current address.

Production mobile analytics setup and required OpenPanel credentials are documented in OpenBot Mobile.

exposes only the Expo development server. It does not expose the local account API, Signal, or TURN. A phone on 5G cannot use the default LAN addresses. For a test across networks, use a VPN that connects both devices, or provide HTTPS and WSS endpoints that forward to this dev stack's account API and Signal ports. Set OPENBOT_MOBILE_AUTH_API_URL to the reachable account API origin and to the reachable Signal URL, including , before starting . Use the ports reported by ; they can differ between worktrees. If direct WebRTC cannot connect, must name a reachable coturn service and must match that service. An HTTP tunnel cannot forward TURN traffic. Generate and scan a new Mobile Connect code after changing the account API address; an existing mobile session retains its original address.

Mobile sign-out removes the local login even when the account API is unavailable. The app keeps only the credential in secure storage for revocation retries at startup, on return to the foreground, and on the next connection attempt. Remote revocation completes when the account API is reachable.

For manual team testing, starts a complete two-client harness. The second client uses the OpenBot Dev Test Client wt-<hash> profile of this worktree ( with ) and renderer port 5174. removes the shared one and the legacy profile. It does not remove the downloaded provider CLIs, which the whole computer shares. Press in the runner terminal to stop only the processes started by that runner, or run from the worktree once that terminal is gone. Never stop a dev stack with or : on a machine running several worktrees those kill the other checkouts' work mid-write, which is what and exist to make unnecessary.

Set OPENBOT_DEV_ICE_TRANSPORT_POLICY=relay before this command to force Team API traffic through coturn. This test option works only with the development renderer. Production always starts with .

The normal command is offline and uses a fake App Server. Manual smoke scripts may use the signed-in subscription and must not run in CI.

Local agents run with the providers' unrestricted execution modes. Each agent starts in its own persistent ~/OpenBot/Agents/<agent-id> workspace and also receives ; routine command and filesystem work in both locations runs without OpenBot adding another permission boundary. Because these modes are intentionally unrestricted, they also permit host access outside those directories when the provider and operating system allow it.

macOS remote desktop permissions

For each macOS account, log in to its GUI session and open Server Settings → Remote desktop access. Select to read Sunshine's Screen Recording and Accessibility permissions, display availability, and GUI session status. The panel names the Mac and the account that runs Sunshine. Grant permissions in that account, including when the account was created with the tenant setup script.

After you publish a server on a Mac, an optional prompt opens this panel. Select to keep using the published server without remote desktop setup.

Use the permission buttons to open System Settings → Privacy & Security on the host. If Sunshine is missing from a list, select and add the bundled with the button. macOS can attribute access to the application that starts Sunshine; enable the application named by the system prompt. Return to OpenBot to check again. If a restart is required, end remote sessions first. A check never restarts an active session.

Select for a local test. If native checks are unavailable, it tests video only and disables viewer input. After the checks pass, it can test mouse and keyboard too. Select from another computer for a remote test. The test requires an otherwise unused remote desktop host. It opens a temporary host panel, keeps remote input inside that panel, and asks you to click a target and type a four-digit code. Confirm that the picture is visible, then select . Local input does not pass the mouse or keyboard test. The panel expires after two minutes. Older hosts or native runtimes require an update before these checks are available.

The native runtime source change invalidates prior artifact pins. The CI workflow builds and tests the new source, then publishes and pins verified artifacts through its existing release flow. Do not reuse old artifact hashes with the new source digest.

Electron main
├── local Codex App Server process over stdio JSONL
├── local Claude Agent SDK session over stream JSON
├── SQLite command log and read projections
├── secure typed IPC handlers
└── sandboxed WebContentsView browser host
    ↕ typed preload bridge
SolidJS renderer

Cloudflare Workers
└── TanStack Start + Solid 2 account API
    ├── D1 accounts, email challenges, hashed sessions, and team tunnels
    └── R2 account avatars
  • owns the Electron lifecycle, window security, local protocol, and IPC registration.
  • owns provider adapters, persistence, message scheduling, transfers, and the browser host.
  • exposes only the typed API.
  • contains the SolidJS interface.
  • contains the TanStack Start account API, one-time email codes, rate limits, and D1 migrations. It also serves the public site: the landing page, , , and the plugin pages at and .
  • contains the public status page at , the script that the workflow runs to check the services, and the script that sends the status webhooks of the team. GitHub hosts it, so it stays up when Cloudflare does not.
  • contains process-boundary contracts, shared limits, and pure validation.
  • contains the interface text in English, French, Japanese, Brazilian Portuguese and Turkish for desktop, web and mobile. See docs/i18n.md to add text or a language.

Attach MP3 audio and MOV video through the file picker or drag and drop. The limits are 100 MB per file, 250 MB per message, and 10 files per message. OpenBot gives the agent the original file; it does not play, decode, transcribe, or validate the recording during import. Damaged recordings can be attached for inspection. Analysis depends on the tools available to the agent. For other audio or video formats, export as MP3, MOV, or MP4, or attach a text transcript. Remote hosts must advertise the capability; update the host if this feature is unavailable.

MP4 video uses the same limits and rules as MOV. Remote hosts must also advertise the capability.

ZIP archives use the same limits. OpenBot does not extract or inspect an archive: the agent gets the original file and extracts it with its own tools. An agent sends a ZIP archive back with openbot.attach_files_to_response, and the user downloads it from the chat. Open shows a ZIP archive in the file manager instead of opening it. Remote hosts must advertise the capability.

Local data and network boundaries

  • ~/OpenBot/Agents/<agent-id> — one working directory per agent. A profile written before the bot-to-agent rename holds them under ; the app moves them on first launch, and a workspace whose move could not run stays readable where it is.
  • — files intentionally shared between agents.
  • ~/OpenBot/Shared/Transfers — managed message snapshots and generated files. Each transfer has an manifest with ownership, recipients, size, and SHA-256 metadata.
  • — embedded-browser downloads.
  • Electron — the canonical OpenBot event log and projections for agents, conversations, provider session bindings, queues, reactions, and attachment indexes.
  • Electron userData/legacy-backup-v1 — unchanged copies of imported and files, when these files existed before the SQLite migration.
  • ~/Library/Application Support/OpenBot/provider-runtimes — the provider CLIs OpenBot downloads and pins. One store for the whole computer, outside any one profile, so every development profile and the packaged app read the same download. keeps the store in that directory instead, so an explicitly named profile stays self-contained.
  • — login and thread history managed exclusively by Codex CLI.
  • — login and session history managed exclusively by Claude CLI.
  • — login and session history managed exclusively by Grok CLI.
  • (or ) — login and session history managed exclusively by the Antigravity ACP server that Gemini uses.
  • — login and session history managed exclusively by the Cursor CLI. A confined Cursor process keeps its settings in ~/.cursor/openbot-confined, so it never changes yours.
  • (or ) — login and session history managed exclusively by the Cline CLI.

Deleting an agent removes its workspace, owned generated attachments, and deliveries addressed only to that agent. A transfer remains when another agent still uses the same message.

OpenBot keeps one stable local conversation when an agent changes between Codex, Grok, and Claude. Native provider session identifiers stay private and are used only to resume provider runtime state.

The Electron renderer is never exposed as a public website. It communicates with local CLI processes over stdio. When the owner publishes OpenBot, its authenticated Team API stays on localhost. WebRTC protocol v3 carries RPC, events, and binary files to desktop and mobile clients. Expo Go hosts the mobile in a hidden Expo DOM component, so mobile uses the same encrypted transport without a custom native development build. The account flow connects to the configured HTTPS Cloudflare API. The client stores only an encrypted OpenBot session token. One-time codes expire after 10 minutes and are stored only as hashes. A daily maintenance task removes expired or consumed authentication records from D1. The embedded browser uses a separate sandboxed Electron session and cannot access or managed local attachments.

To trigger routines from external services, see Webhooks. Public webhook requests require the host to be online.

Read SECURITY.md before reporting a vulnerability. Do not put credentials, private files, conversation contents, or sensitive diagnostics in a public issue.

Full local access is an explicit current product decision, not a security boundary. Reports are especially useful when remote content can reach Electron privileges, managed attachment paths can escape their roots, IPC sender validation can be bypassed, or an agent can act outside the access described above.

Releases are tag-driven. , , or prepares the version and changelog. After review, commit, preflight, and tag the release; pushing the tag builds a signed and notarized macOS ARM64 and x64 release, a signed Windows x64 release, and unsigned Linux x64 and arm64 AppImages in GitHub Actions. After the release is published, the workflow pushes the Docker image to ghcr.io/nightly-labs/openbot. Installed builds check GitHub Releases for updates and expose download/restart controls in the account popover. Release signing secrets and the complete procedure are documented in docs/RELEASING.md.

For one native Standard user per tenant, install the normal OpenBot DMG and the optional OpenBot-Host-<VERSION>-arm64.pkg from the same release. The Host package provides sudo openbot-host setup --create-user client-acme --create-user client-bravo and . sudo openbot-host status [--json] and show the update phase, the staged version, and each tenant's work state. No Git checkout, Bun, or compilation is required on the host. Normal desktop users need only the DMG. See the host deployment guide for existing-user enrollment, password handling, package upgrades, and required target-host checks.

items.title: NVIDIA/SkillSpector
items.content:
Security scanner for AI agent skills. Detect vulnerabilities, malicious patterns, security risks, prompt injection, data exfiltration, and supply-chain risks in Claude Code, Codex, and MCP skills before you install them.

Security scanner for AI agent skills. Detect vulnerabilities, malicious patterns, and security risks before installing agent skills.

AI agent skills (used by Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, etc.) execute with implicit trust and minimal vetting. In the 31,132-skill analyzed subset of the research dataset, 26.1% of skills contain vulnerabilities and 5.2% show likely malicious intent.

SkillSpector helps you answer: "Is this skill safe to install?"

  • : Scan Git repos, URLs, zip files, directories, or single files
  • 71 vulnerability patterns across 17 categories: prompt injection, data exfiltration, privilege escalation, supply chain, excessive agency, output handling, system prompt leakage, memory poisoning, tool misuse, rogue agent, anti-refusal, trigger abuse, dangerous code (AST), taint tracking, YARA signatures, MCP least privilege, and MCP tool poisoning
  • : Fast static analysis + optional LLM semantic evaluation
  • Live vulnerability lookups: SC4 queries OSV.dev for real-time CVE data with automatic offline fallback
  • : Terminal, JSON, Markdown, and SARIF reports
  • : 0-100 score with severity labels and clear recommendations
  • Baseline / false-positive suppression: Accept known findings via a glob-rule or fingerprint baseline so re-scans surface only issues (docs)

Open-source software notice: This project will download and install additional third-party open source software projects. Review the license terms of these open source projects before use.

Create and activate a virtual environment first (all targets assume the venv is active). Use or ; the Makefile uses if available, otherwise .

Quick install with uv (CLI-only):

uv tool install git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git
# Update later: uv tool update skillspector

If you plan to run , install the MCP extra at install time:

uv tool install 'skillspector[mcp] @ git+https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git'

# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/NVIDIA/skillspector.git
cd skillspector

# Create and activate virtual environment
uv venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate
# or: python3 -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate

# Install for production use
make install

# Or install with development dependencies
make install-dev

Docker (no Python required)

Run SkillSpector without installing Python by building it locally from the included Dockerfile. The image is based on the Docker Official Python image.

make docker-build
# or: docker build -t skillspector .

by mounting your current directory into , the container's working directory:

docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/scan" skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --no-llm

by passing credentials with a local file:

cat > .env <<'EOF'
SKILLSPECTOR_PROVIDER=anthropic
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...
EOF

docker run --rm \
  -v "$PWD:/scan" \
  --env-file .env \
  skillspector scan ./my-skill/

Or pass credentials directly from your shell environment:

docker run --rm \
  -v "$PWD:/scan" \
  -e SKILLSPECTOR_PROVIDER=anthropic \
  -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY="$ANTHROPIC_API_KEY" \
  skillspector scan ./my-skill/

Write a report to the host filesystem by writing to the mounted directory:

docker run --rm --user "$(id -u):$(id -g)" \
  -v "$PWD:/scan" \
  skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --no-llm --format json --output report.json

for repeated static scans:

alias skillspector-docker='docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/scan" skillspector'
skillspector-docker scan ./my-skill/ --no-llm

# Scan a local skill directory
skillspector scan ./my-skill/

# Scan a single SKILL.md file
skillspector scan ./SKILL.md

# Scan a Git repository
skillspector scan https://github.com/user/my-skill

# Scan a zip file
skillspector scan ./my-skill.zip

SkillSpector enforces two independent caps on remote and archive inputs to bound the impact of oversized downloads and zip bombs:

  • : (100 MiB) — applied to streamed URL downloads, total uncompressed size of zip archives, and post-clone disk usage of Git repos.
  • : (10,000) — caps the number of entries in a single zip.

Note that the per-file 1 MB analysis cap () is a separate, downstream limit: it bounds what individual analyzers will read out of an already-ingested directory. The ingest caps above bound how much content can land on disk in the first place. A breach of either ingest cap fails closed with an .

# Terminal output (default) - pretty formatted
skillspector scan ./my-skill/

# JSON output - machine readable
skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --format json --output report.json

# Markdown output - for documentation
skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --format markdown --output report.md

# SARIF output - for CI/CD integration and IDE tooling
skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --format sarif --output report.sarif

Scan entire directories of skills in parallel from :

python -m contrib.batch_scan.batch_scan ./my-skills/ --no-llm
python -m contrib.batch_scan.batch_scan ./my-skills/ --workers 20 -f json -o report.json
python -m contrib.batch_scan.batch_scan ./tests/fixtures/ -f terminal --workers 20

Supports multilingual detection (zh/ja/ko) and terminal/JSON/Markdown output.

For LLM scans with higher concurrency, configure multiple API keys following — the pool improves throughput and resilience, provided the keys don't share an account-level rate limit.

The default configuration targets DeepSeek as the cheapest public option. DeepSeek-Chat is expected to sunset, and the contributor does not have hardware to test against local models. The batch scanner was originally tested with OpenAI-compatible endpoints — DeepSeek's lack of structured-output support required manual JSON-parsing patches. If you can contribute a more universal backend (Ollama, vLLM, or a different provider), PRs are very welcome.

Comparing MCP Registry snapshots

Start with raw registry payload captures ( and ). Save a scan report as , then compare a later scan against that generated local report:

skillspector scan registry-before.json --mcp-registry --format json --output previous.json
skillspector scan registry-after.json --mcp-registry --format json \
  --mcp-registry-compare previous.json --output compared.json

The optional object lists added and removed server identities, changed normalized fields with their previous and current values, and an . Identity is the server name and version, so a new version appears as an addition and the old version as a removal if it is absent from the new scan. Acquisition source and scan timestamp are excluded from comparison. lists same-identity records whose raw-record hash changed while normalized fields match; these are not counted as unchanged. This can indicate a change to fields outside the snapshot model, or array reordering in the raw record. Package and remote ordering alone is not a normalized field change. Entries in may also contain changes outside the snapshot model; inspect the raw record to see those changes. Compare reports with the same selection scope: a server absent from the current input is reported as removed, which does not prove it was removed from a registry.

The comparison file must be a local report produced by this registry mode with valid normalized snapshots. Malformed, oversized or duplicate server identities are rejected. This option requires and is separate from the finding-suppression : it never suppresses findings or changes risk scores, and it does not fetch or execute listed server endpoints.

Registry mode rejects skill-only controls such as , , , --transitive-allow-prefix, and with exit code 2, including an explicitly supplied default depth (). Omit these options for registry scans.

Suppressing False Positives (baseline)

Suppress known/accepted findings so the risk score reflects only un-triaged issues and re-scans surface only findings. See the suppression guide for the full reference.

# Accept all current findings into a baseline (run once), then commit it.
skillspector baseline ./my-skill/ -o .skillspector-baseline.yaml

# Scan against the baseline — only NEW findings are reported and scored.
skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --baseline .skillspector-baseline.yaml

# Review what was suppressed (still excluded from the score).
skillspector scan ./my-skill/ --baseline .skillspector-baseline.yaml --show-suppressed

A baseline can also use drift-tolerant glob rules (by rule id, file path, or message) — see .skillspector-baseline.example.yaml. Exact fingerprint baselines are evidence-bound: changing the scanned source or SkillSpector version keeps the finding active until it is reviewed again. When a selected baseline or baseline output is stored inside the skill directory, SkillSpector excludes that exact file from content analysis so its suppression text cannot create findings or enter regenerated fingerprints; sibling files remain in normal scan scope.

For a local directory containing one or , repeat to omit selected files before content analysis:

skillspector scan ./my-skill --exclude 'tests/*' --exclude 'fixtures/*.json'

Patterns are case-sensitive globs matched against the entire relative POSIX path; also matches . Quote patterns so your shell does not expand them. This is an explicit caller option, not an author-controlled ignore file. Patterns matching either manifest name ( or ) are rejected, as are recursive, multi-skill, transitive, registry, and non-directory inputs. No-match patterns are still recorded in the report.

Files already outside the scan inventory, such as policy-excluded dependencies, retain their existing policy handling and are not counted as caller exclusions. Explicitly excluded inventory files remain in the coverage denominator as entirely uninspected. The report lists the applied patterns, excluded count and individual skipped paths; any matched exclusion makes coverage partial and prevents a recommendation. Use when partial scope should fail CI. These exclusions do not suppress findings in included files or override existing safety limits.

Structured output is requested through LangChain's . The default is client-specific: uses , while other clients may use tool calling. Some models reject a forced tool call with HTTP 400 (tool_choice: type "tool" and "any" are not supported for this model). The and providers route those models (, , , , or any registry entry with structured_output: json_schema) to the native JSON-schema response format. Bedrock has no JSON-schema output for them, so the provider leaves at , asks for the tool call in the prompt, and retries a prose answer; it recognises the model from the model ID, a geo/global inference-profile ID, or a foundation-model / inference-profile ARN. An application-inference-profile ARN hides the model, so add that ARN to the registry (SKILLSPECTOR_MODEL_REGISTRY) with . The provider honours the same entry for endpoints that ignore both and a forced and answer in prose (for example iFlytek's , which is bundled). The , , , and providers also recognise those Claude models inside gateway model IDs such as anthropic/claude-opus-5-5 or aws/anthropic/bedrock-claude-opus-5-5. Some OpenAI-compatible gateways turn a response format for Claude into a forced tool call, so the and providers bind the schema as a tool with left at and retry a prose answer. SKILLSPECTOR_STRUCTURED_OUTPUT_METHOD=json_schema|function_calling overrides the method for any provider. The method precedence is SKILLSPECTOR_STRUCTURED_OUTPUT_METHOD, the provider's method hint, an analyzer preference, then the client default. TP4 prefers only for provider and the exact model label azure/anthropic/claude-opus-5, with reasoning/thinking controls unset; dated or suffixed labels and other providers keep their existing behavior. An explicit environment override or provider hint still wins when reasoning is configured.

Security — HTTP transport trust model

The HTTP transport ships . Any caller that can reach the port can invoke . HTTP bindings are restricted to loopback IPs ( or ); binds to without DNS resolution. Wildcard, routable and other hostname bindings are rejected.

  • For remote access, put an authenticating reverse proxy (e.g. nginx + mTLS) in front of the loopback listener.
  • Local paths and URLs are over HTTP to prevent unauthenticated callers from reading arbitrary host files. Only remote Git and URLs are accepted.

HTTP scans accept only credential-free targets. Git scans never use the server's Git login or Git config. If a proxy or custom CA is needed, set , or in the server environment. Use stdio or the CLI for private repositories. Git redirects are rejected; use the current repository URL after a rename or transfer.

SkillSpector uses a two-stage detection pipeline:

  • Fast regex-based pattern matching across 11 static analyzers
  • AST-based behavioral analysis detecting dangerous calls (exec, eval, subprocess, etc.)
  • Live vulnerability lookups via OSV.dev for known CVEs in dependencies
  • Scans all analyzer-eligible files in the skill
  • High recall (catches most issues)
  • Moderate precision (some false positives)

OpenSSF Model Signing / DSSE bundles remain in content analysis, regardless of filename. Static and LLM analyzers inspect decoded JSON payloads, readable DER certificate/signature content, and all unknown wrapper fields. Strictly parsed binary fields are projected rather than treated as executable base64; canonical bytes remain available to YARA and fingerprints. Unsupported encodings (including environments without the optional dependency) retain raw fields and produce an explicit incomplete-analysis warning. Findings in decoded content point to the original bundle and label their projection in evidence. None of this verifies signatures, certificate chains, transparency logs, or signer identity.

Stage 2: LLM Semantic Analysis (Optional)

  • Evaluates context and intent
  • Confirmed findings may gain an explanation and higher confidence, never lower
  • Every deterministic finding stays in the report whether the model confirms it, disputes it, or does not address it
  • Findings the model reviews but does not confirm (disputed, low-confidence, or unaddressed) are tagged in JSON and SARIF output
  • Findings whose review fails are kept without that tag; evidence.llm_review_outcome distinguishes , , , , and in JSON and SARIF output
  • Results depend on the configured model and prompt context; Stage 2 does not replace deterministic findings or guarantee a particular precision rate

The LLM prompt includes anti-jailbreak protections to prevent malicious skills from manipulating the analysis.

Live Vulnerability Lookups (SC4)

SC4 uses the OSV.dev API to check dependencies against the full Open Source Vulnerabilities database — covering tens of thousands of advisories across PyPI and npm.

  • — OSV.dev is free and unauthenticated.
  • — all dependencies are checked in a single HTTP call.
  • — if OSV.dev is unreachable (air-gapped/offline), a small built-in fallback list is used.
  • — results are cached in-memory for 1 hour to avoid redundant API calls during a session.

The tool requires outbound HTTPS access to for live vulnerability data. When that is not available, findings are limited to the static fallback list.

Trust model and data egress

SkillSpector is defense-in-depth, not a sandbox. Know what it does and does not do before relying on it:

  • It never executes the scanned skill. All analysis is static (regex, Python AST, YARA) plus optional LLM evaluation of file — the skill's code is never run.
  • LLM analysis sends analyzer-eligible file contents to the configured provider. When LLM analysis is enabled (the default), file contents are sent to the active endpoint. DSSE payloads and readable signing metadata are included. Use to keep contents local (static analysis only).
  • SC4 sends dependency names to OSV.dev. The supply-chain check queries OSV.dev with the package names and versions the skill declares, to look up known CVEs. This is fundamental to the check and runs even with . It sends dependency coordinates (not file contents), requires no API key, and falls back to a bundled list when OSV.dev is unreachable.
  • It does not sandbox the host. SkillSpector flags risky patterns you install a skill; it does not contain or isolate a skill you choose to install anyway.
  • : May miss patterns in other languages
  • : Cannot analyze text in images
  • : Cannot analyze compiled or encrypted content
  • : Static analysis only, no dynamic execution
  • : Without network access to , SC4 uses a small static fallback list

Based on research from "Agent Skills in the Wild: An Empirical Study of Security Vulnerabilities at Scale" (Liu et al., 2026):

  • : 42,447 skills from major marketplaces; 31,132 were analyzed for the following rates
  • : 26.1% of the analyzed subset contain at least one vulnerability
  • : 5.2% of the analyzed subset show likely malicious intent
  • : Skills with executable scripts are 2.12x more likely to be vulnerable
from skillspector import graph

# Invoke the LangGraph workflow
result = graph.invoke({
    "input_path": "/path/to/skill",
    "output_format": "json",   # terminal, json, markdown, or sarif
    "use_llm": True,           # False for static-only analysis
})

# Access results
print(f"Risk Score: {result['risk_score']}/100")
print(f"Severity: {result['risk_severity']}")
print(f"Recommendation: {result['risk_recommendation']}")

for finding in result["filtered_findings"]:
    print(f"[{finding['severity']}] {finding['rule_id']}: {finding['message']}")

You can use a VPS, a bare-metal server, a Raspberry Pi, or any other server that accepts SSH connections. Coolify gives you the convenience of a cloud platform while you keep control of your infrastructure.

  • Integrate with your workflow: Manage resources through the dashboard, API, CLI, MCP, and team-based access controls.
